UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle
UNIT.content:
• Area of a sector — deriving and applying the formula (θ/360 × πr²) using paper cut-outs of sectors with measured radius and included angle
• Area of a segment — computing area of a segment by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of the corresponding sector
• Applications of area of part of a circle in real-life situations — designing patterns, cutting circular fruits (e.g. watermelon), area swept by an opening door, decorative surfaces
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) determine the area of a sector of a circle in different situations,
b) determine the area of a segment of a circle in different situations,
c) apply the area of part of a circle in real-life situations,
d) appreciate the application of area of part of circular objects in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner explores different options of improvising cut-outs of sectors of a circle for working out their areas, and selects appropriate formulas when solving problems involving sectors and segments.
• Learning to Learn: the learner acquires new knowledge as they discuss with peers how to work out areas of circular objects, and independently investigates the relationship between a sector and its corresponding triangle to derive the segment area formula.
• Citizenship: learners appreciate their immediate environment as they gather locally available circular objects (e.g. sufuria lids, clock faces, wheel hubs) and use them to explore real-life applications of circular area.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: The learner exhibits devotion and honesty by undertaking tasks while working with peers to make paper cut-outs of sectors of a circle and obtain measurements, sharing resources equitably within the group.
• Peace: the learner displays care and tolerance while discussing with peers and obtaining circular objects, tracing and marking out sectors and segments, and respecting differing approaches to problem-solving.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: learners pose questions about why a slice of watermelon or a swept floor area is not a simple rectangle or triangle, driving investigation into circular area formulas.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: learners design and execute a hands-on cut-out activity — measuring radius and central angle of paper sectors, recording data in a table, and computing areas to verify the formula.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: learners apply the sector and segment area formulas (θ/360 × πr²; sector area minus triangle area) to solve quantitative problems set in Kenyan contexts.
• Constructing Explanations: learners articulate why the formula for a sector is a fraction of the full circle's area, linking the central angle to the proportion of the circle, and explain the segment derivation step-by-step.
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: learners present their findings on real-life applications (door sweeps, watermelon slices, wiper blade arcs) to peers and evaluate each other's reasoning.
UNIT.pcis:
• Education for Sustainable Development: the learner uses locally available circular objects (sufuria lids, tin can bases, clock faces found in Nairobi markets) to trace and mark out sectors and segments, minimising waste by repurposing materials as learning resources.
• Life Skills (Decision Making): the learner makes informed decisions when selecting appropriate formulas and methods for calculating the area of a sector or segment in varied real-life problem contexts.
UNIT.careers:
• Architecture and Interior Design: calculating the floor area swept by doors and designing circular decorative patterns on buildings in cities like Nairobi and Mombasa requires accurate sector and segment area computations.
• Hospitality and Catering: portioning circular foods (watermelon, mandazi rounds, cake) into equal or specified sector-shaped servings requires understanding sector angles and areas — directly relevant to Kenya's hospitality industry.
• Sports Management and Coaching: computing the area of circular sectors on athletic tracks and field event circles (e.g. discus throwing sector) at venues such as Nyayo Stadium uses sector area concepts.
• Journalism and Photography: framing circular graphic elements, pie-chart overlays, and camera aperture calculations in media production connect to arc and sector proportions.
• Agriculture and Land Management: parcelling circular irrigation plots or rotational grazing paddocks in the Rift Valley into sector-shaped portions requires applying area of a sector to real land areas.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to calculate and apply the area of sectors and segments of a circle, building directly on prior knowledge of circle properties and polygon areas (Sub-Strand 2.4). Learners progress from hands-on paper cut-out investigations to abstract formula derivation and finally to solving authentic Kenyan real-life problems. The unit foregrounds collaborative inquiry, local material use, and the utility of mathematics in everyday contexts such as food portioning, door clearance planning, and decorative design.
UNIT.phenomenon: A mama mboga at Wakulima Market in Nairobi slices a large, perfectly circular watermelon into unequal wedge-shaped pieces to sell by the slice. Some customers complain that their pieces look smaller than others even though the vendor claims she cut the melon fairly. A student notices that two pieces cut at different angles but with the same radius look very different in size — one is a thin sliver and another is a wide wedge. The puzzle: the pieces are all bounded by two straight cuts and a curved rind, yet their sizes are clearly different. Why does changing only the angle of the cut change the area of the piece so dramatically? How can we calculate exactly how much watermelon (in cm²) is in any given wedge so that every customer truly gets a fair share? This is puzzling because learners' prior experience with area (rectangles, triangles, polygons) gives them no direct method for handling a shape bounded by two radii and a curved arc.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A watchman at a school gate in Kisumu notices that the open gate sweeps a fan-shaped region on the ground as it swings from closed to fully open — the painted warning zone on the ground is sector-shaped; how much ground area must be kept clear?
• A matatu windscreen wiper in Mombasa clears a sector-shaped region of glass with each sweep; the driver wants to know how much of the windscreen is actually cleaned and how much remains obscured — this involves the area of a sector (and of the uncleaned segment near the pivot).
• A craftsperson in Kericho making decorative leather coasters cuts circular discs and then removes a circular segment from each to create a "D-shaped" coaster — calculating how much leather is wasted per coaster requires segment area.
• A farmer in the Rift Valley installs a centre-pivot irrigation system that rotates through a 270° arc; the county water office needs to know the irrigated area in hectares to allocate water rights — this is a direct sector-area calculation on a large scale.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped or segment-shaped piece of a circle — like a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market — so that we can solve fair-sharing and design problems in real life?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT: Anchoring Phenomenon Launch (Sector intuition)
Learners are shown a large paper circle representing a watermelon cross-section. The teacher poses the driving question and asks learners to predict (individually, in writing) which of three drawn sectors — with angles 45°, 90°, and 135° and the same radius — has the largest area and by approximately how much. Cold-call 4 learners to share predictions; record on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Learners then discuss in pairs: what information would you need to calculate the exact area of each slice? Introduce vocabulary: sector, radius, central angle, arc.

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE: Investigating Sector Area with Cut-Outs
Learners work in groups of 4. Each group receives a printed circle (radius 7 cm), a protractor, scissors, and a ruler. Groups cut out sectors of specified angles (30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) and arrange them side by side. They measure and record radius and angle, then calculate each sector's area as a fraction of the full circle area (πr²). Groups tabulate results and identify the pattern: Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². Teacher circulates, asking targeted questions: "What fraction of the full circle is your 90° sector?" WAIT TIME: 30 seconds after each question before cold-calling.

Lesson 3 — EXPLAIN: Deriving and Applying the Sector Area Formula
Teacher formalises the sector area formula from the groups' findings. Learners work through three graduated examples in Kenyan contexts: (1) a 120° slice of a watermelon of radius 15 cm; (2) the area swept by a school gate of radius 1.2 m swinging through 75°; (3) a centre-pivot irrigation arc of radius 80 m through 270°. Pairs solve problems and present solutions; class evaluates. Learners update the DQB with the sector formula and one new question that has arisen.

Lesson 4 — OBSERVE: Investigating Segment Area
Learners return to their sector cut-outs. Teacher guides: "Inside this sector, there is a triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. What shape is left if we remove that triangle?" Learners cut out the triangle (base = chord, two equal sides = radius) from the sector to isolate the segment. They measure dimensions, calculate triangle area (½r²sinθ), and subtract from sector area to find segment area. Groups record the formula: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. Observation schedule used for group work assessment.

Lesson 5 — EXPLAIN: Applying the Segment Area Formula
Teacher works through two fully worked examples: (1) finding the area of the segment of a circle of radius 10 cm with a chord subtending 60° at the centre (context: leather coaster waste in Kericho); (2) the area of glass NOT cleaned by a matatu wiper of radius 30 cm that sweeps 110° (the uncleaned segment near the pivot). Learners then attempt two problems independently. WAIT TIME: allow 5 minutes silent work before peer discussion. Cold-call 3 learners to present solutions on the board. Correct misconceptions around the subtraction step.

Lesson 6 — DRIVING QUESTION BOARD (DQB) Update + Mixed Practice
Learners revisit the DQB, answer questions resolved so far (sector formula, segment formula), and post new "wonder" questions. Teacher facilitates a class discussion linking back to the anchoring phenomenon: "Can we now calculate whether the mama mboga's slices are truly equal?" Learners calculate and compare three watermelon slice areas (angles 40°, 55°, 75°; radius 18 cm) and write a short justification of fairness. Introduce mixed problems combining both sector and segment in one context (e.g. total area of a decorative window panel in a Nairobi mosque).

Lesson 7 — MODEL BUILDING: Real-Life Design Task
Learners work in pairs on a design challenge: plan a circular flowerbed of radius 2 m in the school compound that is divided into 4 sector-shaped sections for different plants; one section must be exactly 25% of the total area, two sections must be equal, and the fourth section is the remainder. Learners must calculate and label the angle and area of each section. Extension: one pair calculates the area of a decorative stone path that forms a segment around the outer edge of one section. Learners produce a labelled diagram with all calculations shown.

Lesson 8 — SUMMATIVE REVIEW + MODEL PRESENTATION
Groups present their flowerbed designs and calculations to the class; peers provide structured feedback using the KICD assessment rubric criteria (sector area, segment area, application). Teacher conducts a whole-class consolidation: revisit the driving question with final answers, review the DQB for any unresolved questions, and administer a short written class activity (4 questions: 1 sector, 1 segment, 1 application, 1 multi-step). Learners reflect in their portfolios on what changed in their thinking from Lesson 1 to Lesson 8 regarding the watermelon phenomenon.

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon by confronting learners with the puzzle of why watermelon wedges cut from the same circular melon at different angles have dramatically different areas, and to surface prior knowledge and initial intuitions about area.
slo.knowledge:
• A sector is the region bounded by two radii and an arc of a circle.
• The central angle (angle at the centre) is the key variable that determines the size of a sector when the radius is fixed.
• Prior area methods (rectangles, triangles, polygons) cannot be directly applied to shapes bounded by a curved edge.
slo.skills:
• Estimate and compare areas of sector-shaped pieces using reasoning and visual inspection.
• Formulate mathematical questions arising from a real-life fair-sharing problem.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematics is embedded in everyday Kenyan market activities.
• Show curiosity and intellectual honesty when prior knowledge is insufficient to solve a new problem.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson that anchors the entire sub-strand in the Wakulima Market watermelon phenomenon; it surfaces learners' intuitions about sector area, exposes the gap in their prior knowledge, and launches the Driving Question Board that will be built upon throughout the sub-strand.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. If a physical watermelon or knife is brought to class for demonstration, the teacher only handles the cutting implement; learners observe from their seats and do not handle any sharp objects.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson opens the Area of Part of a Circle sub-strand by immersing Grade 10 learners in a vivid, locally grounded phenomenon: a mama mboga at Wakulima Market in Nairobi slicing a large circular watermelon into unequal wedge-shaped pieces. Some customers complain that their pieces look smaller, yet the vendor insists the cuts are fair. Learners are immediately invited to take a position — before any instruction — on which piece is larger and why. This predict-first approach deliberately surfaces the misconception that equal-looking cuts are equal in area, and exposes the critical variable of central angle.

In the Observe phase, learners examine printed or projected sector cut-outs drawn on centimetre-square grid paper, all with the same radius (7 cm, a clean number that later connects to the formula A = θ/360 × πr²) but with central angles of 30°, 90°, 120°, and 180°. By counting grid squares, learners generate raw area estimates for each piece. This concrete counting activity creates a need for a more efficient method and plants the seed that area grows in proportion to the central angle — the key conceptual insight of the sub-strand.

The lesson closes by constructing the class Driving Question Board (DQB), where learners post their burning questions and initial models (rough sketches annotating what they think controls sector size). This DQB will be revisited and updated in every subsequent lesson, giving learners a visible record of their growing understanding. No formula is introduced in Lesson 1; the lesson's sole purpose is to create genuine intellectual need for the mathematics that follows.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners view a projected image (or teacher-drawn sketch on the board) showing a large circular watermelon divided into four wedge-shaped pieces — all with the same radius but with central angles of 30°, 90°, 120°, and 180°. Each piece is labelled A, B, C, and D respectively. Individually and silently, learners write in their exercise books: (1) a ranking of the four pieces from smallest to largest area, and (2) one sentence explaining what they think makes one piece bigger than another. After 2 minutes, learners share their ranking with a partner using a Think-Pair-Share protocol before a whole-class discussion.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the watermelon diagram and say: 'Mama Wanjiku sells watermelon slices at Wakulima Market every Saturday. She cut this melon into four pieces — A, B, C, and D. A customer is complaining that piece B is much smaller than piece D. Mama Wanjiku says all her cuts are from the same melon, the same size. Who is right? In your book, rank these pieces from smallest to largest and write ONE sentence: what makes a piece big or small?' Allow WAIT TIME of 15 seconds before any learner writes, to let the image settle. After 2 minutes of individual writing, say: 'Turn to your neighbour — 60 seconds — compare your rankings.' After pair discussion, cold-call 4 learners (choose one high-confidence, one hesitant, one who ranked differently from the majority, one who mentioned 'angle' unprompted) using the prompt: 'Tell us your ranking and your reason.' Record all four rankings on the board without evaluating correctness. Then ask the class: 'We have four different rankings on the board. They cannot all be right. What information would help us decide?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME before taking 3 hands.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with public ranking display. By posting all four rankings without judgment, the teacher creates productive controversy — learners can see that the class does not yet have a shared, justified answer. This cognitive dissonance is the engine that drives motivation through the rest of the lesson and the sub-strand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written rankings as learners work (circulate, read 6–8 books). Key indicator: Do learners mention 'angle', 'width of the cut', or 'how open the piece is' in their explanations? Learners who rely only on visual impression ('it looks bigger') have not yet identified the relevant variable. Note these learners for targeted questioning in the Observe phase. Record on a mental checklist: proportion of class who named the central angle as the key variable (expected: fewer than 30% at this stage).

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner (or pair of learners if resources are limited) receives a printed A4 sheet showing four sector cut-outs drawn accurately on a 1 cm² grid: Sector A (r = 7 cm, θ = 30°), Sector B (r = 7 cm, θ = 90°), Sector C (r = 7 cm, θ = 120°), and Sector D (r = 7 cm, θ = 180°). Learners count grid squares inside each sector (counting a partial square ≥ half as 1, and < half as 0) and record their estimates in a four-row table in their books with columns: Sector | Central Angle (°) | Estimated Area (cm²). They then answer two guided questions: 'What stays the same across all four pieces?' and 'What is different?'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the grid sheets and say: 'Each of these four shapes represents one watermelon slice. They were all cut from a melon with radius 7 cm — the same melon. Your job right now is NOT to use a formula. Count the squares inside each shape as carefully as you can. Record your estimates in your table.' Circulate for 5 minutes. When most learners have at least two rows complete, ask a probing question to the whole class (do not wait for all to finish): 'Without telling me the number yet — as you move from Sector A to Sector D, what is happening to the number of squares?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 learners. Then say: 'Finish your table. You have 3 more minutes.' After counting is complete, direct learners to the two guided questions. Cold-call 2 learners for each question. When a learner answers 'the radius is the same', affirm and press: 'Exactly — and what IS different? What did Mama Wanjiku change each time she made a new cut?' Expect and draw out the answer 'the angle' or 'how wide the cut is.' Write on the board: CENTRAL ANGLE — the angle between the two straight cuts.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Data Collection with Guided Noticing. Counting grid squares is a deliberate bridging strategy: it connects the familiar concept of area-as-square-counting to the unfamiliar curved shape, making the area of a sector tangible and concrete. The two guided questions (same/different) direct learners toward the invariant (radius) and the variable (angle), which is the conceptual core of the formula A = θ/360 × πr².
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher looks for two things during circulation: (1) Are learners' area estimates increasing monotonically from A to D? (Expected: ~38 cm², ~154 cm², ~205 cm², ~308 cm² for r = 7 cm — but grid counting will give rough approximations; the key is the ordering.) A learner whose estimates are not increasing has made a counting error or misidentified the sector boundaries — intervene immediately. (2) In the guided questions, can learners articulate 'central angle' or an equivalent phrase as the varying quantity? This is the exit criterion for conceptual readiness for Lesson 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners use their four area estimates to fill in a proportional reasoning prompt on the board: 'Sector D has angle 180° and Sector B has angle 90°. Sector D's angle is __ times bigger than Sector B's angle. Is Sector D's area approximately __ times bigger than Sector B's area?' Learners check this against their grid counts. They then discuss in groups of three: 'If Mama Wanjiku doubled the angle of a slice — from 60° to 120° — what would happen to the area of the piece? Justify your answer using your table.' Groups share out, and the teacher scribes the emerging conjecture on the board: 'Area of a sector seems to be proportional to the central angle (when the radius is fixed).'
framework.teacherMoves: Write the proportional reasoning prompt on the board and say: 'Look at your table. Sector D has angle 180° and Sector B has angle 90°. 180 is exactly how many times 90?' Pause — 5 seconds WAIT TIME — 'Two times. Now look at your area estimates for D and B. Is the area of D approximately two times the area of B? Check it.' Allow 2 minutes. Cold-call 2 learners: 'What did you find?' After confirming the doubling relationship, pose the group discussion question: 'In your group of three — Mama Wanjiku's customer wants DOUBLE the watermelon. She has a 60° slice. What angle should the new slice be, and how does the area change? You have 90 seconds — go.' After group discussion, cold-call one group to present. Scribe their conjecture verbatim, then say: 'We are NOT proving this today. We are noticing a pattern. Our big question is: can we find an EXACT formula — not just counting squares — so that Mama Wanjiku can calculate the area of any slice to the nearest cm²? That is what we will build together over the next lessons.' Point to the conjecture on the board: 'This is our first clue.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Proportional Reasoning Bridge. By asking learners to check whether doubling the angle doubles the area, the teacher is scaffolding the core mathematical structure of the sector area formula (A ∝ θ) without stating it. This is a sense-making move rather than direct instruction — learners arrive at the proportionality conjecture through their own data, which increases ownership and retention.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens to group discussions for the quality of justification. Target indicator: Can learners use the word 'proportional' or an equivalent idea ('the area goes up by the same amount as the angle goes up') to justify their conjecture? Learners who say only 'it gets bigger' have not yet made the proportionality connection — the teacher should prompt: 'By how MUCH does it get bigger? Check your numbers.' Also note any group that raises the question of what happens when the radius changes — this shows readiness for extension and should be acknowledged publicly: 'Excellent question — that is something we will explore in a later lesson.'

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes (or tears a page into two pieces if sticky notes are unavailable). On the first note, they write one question they still have about the watermelon problem — something they genuinely do not yet know how to answer. On the second note, they write one thing they are now more sure about after the Observe and Explain phases. Learners post their notes on the class DQB (a dedicated section of the board or a large sheet of paper fixed to the wall), grouping them under two columns: 'Questions We Have' and 'Things We Are Starting to Understand.' The teacher reads several questions aloud and organises them into clusters: questions about the formula, questions about what happens when the radius changes, questions about the curved part (arc), and questions about segments versus sectors.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We are going to start our Driving Question Board — this will live on our wall for the whole unit. Every time we learn something new, we will come back and update it.' Distribute sticky notes. 'On your FIRST note, write ONE genuine question you still cannot answer about Mama Wanjiku's watermelon problem. Be specific — not just 'how do you find the area' but WHY does the angle matter? How does the curved rind fit in? On your SECOND note, write one thing you are now more confident about.' Allow 3 minutes of silent writing. Then: 'Come and post your notes.' As learners post, the teacher reads 4–5 questions aloud: 'I see Amina has written: Does the curved part add to the area or is it just the boundary? Excellent — that is going on our DQB. Kevin asks: What if two slices have different radii — can a small angle with a big radius be equal to a big angle with a small radius? Fantastic — that is a deeper question we will return to.' Cluster the questions visibly. Point to the driving question written at the top of the DQB: 'How can we calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped or segment-shaped piece of a circle — like a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market — so that we can solve fair-sharing and design problems in real life?' Say: 'Every question on this board is a step toward answering that driving question. We will not erase a single one — we will answer them one by one.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public Knowledge Tracking via the Driving Question Board. The DQB is a sensemaking artefact that makes the class's collective understanding visible and evolving. By separating 'questions' from 'things we are starting to understand,' the teacher helps learners distinguish between what they know, what they suspect, and what they do not yet know — a metacognitive habit central to the CBE competency of 'learning to learn.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all DQB notes after class. Key diagnostic indicators: (1) Quality of questions — are they about the mathematical structure (angle, radius, formula) or purely procedural ('how do you solve it')? A class dominated by procedural questions has not yet engaged with the phenomenon at a conceptual level. (2) Quality of 'things we are starting to understand' notes — do learners cite specific evidence from the grid-counting activity? Notes that reference the data ('Sector D had about twice the squares as Sector B because the angle was twice as big') show strong sensemaking; vague notes ('area depends on the circle') show surface engagement. Use this diagnostic to adjust the depth of Lesson 2's instruction.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners draw a rough initial model in their books: a circle with a shaded sector, labelled with the two quantities they have identified as relevant (radius r and central angle θ). They annotate the model with an arrow pointing to the shaded region and write their current best conjecture for what controls its area, in their own words. Below the sketch, they write a 'Model Statement': 'I think the area of a watermelon slice depends on ___ and ___ because ___.' This model will be revised in every subsequent lesson as new mathematical tools are acquired.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Scientists and mathematicians build models to capture what they understand so far — even when the model is incomplete. In your book, draw a circle. Shade one sector — one slice. Label the radius r and label the angle in the middle θ (theta) — that is the Greek letter mathematicians use for angles. Now write your Model Statement: I think the area of a watermelon slice depends on ___ and ___ because ___. You have 3 minutes.' Circulate and read 5–6 model statements. Identify one strong model statement to share (ask permission): 'Zawadi wrote: I think the area depends on the angle and the radius because when the angle doubled in our grid activity, the area doubled, and a bigger radius would make a bigger circle to cut from. That is a strong model. Notice she used EVIDENCE from our activity.' Then say: 'This model is NOT finished — it has no formula yet, no numbers, no proof. That is exactly what this unit is about. Every lesson, we will come back and make this model stronger. By the end of this sub-strand, your model will be able to calculate the EXACT area of any slice to the nearest square centimetre — so every customer at Wakulima Market gets a truly fair share.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Model Construction with Annotated Conjecture. Asking learners to build an incomplete model deliberately normalises the scientific practice of modelling under uncertainty. The Model Statement template ('depends on ___ and ___ because ___') requires learners to commit to a claim AND a justification, which is the foundation of mathematical reasoning. Revisiting and revising this model across lessons creates a longitudinal sensemaking thread connecting all lessons in the sub-strand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects or photographs 6–8 model statements at the end of class. Readiness indicator for Lesson 2: Does the learner's model statement correctly identify BOTH radius and central angle as the relevant variables, with a reason grounded in the grid-counting evidence? A learner who identifies only angle (but not radius) is partially correct and will need the extension investigation in Lesson 2. A learner who identifies neither variable and relies on visual impression alone may need a bridging conversation at the start of Lesson 2. Record names of learners in each category for differentiated follow-up.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Predict phase, what proportion of learners spontaneously identified the central angle as the key variable — and what does this tell you about the prior knowledge your class brings to this sub-strand from their work on circles in Junior School?
2. Were learners' grid-counting estimates accurate enough to show a clear monotonic increase from Sector A to Sector D? If not, what does this suggest about their spatial reasoning skills, and how will you address this in Lesson 2?
3. How rich were the questions learners posted on the Driving Question Board? Did they focus on procedural steps, or did they show curiosity about the mathematical structure (why angle matters, what the curved arc contributes)? What does this tell you about the depth of engagement the phenomenon created?
4. In the Model Building phase, could learners justify their Model Statements with reference to evidence from the activity, or did they rely on intuition alone? What scaffolding will you provide in Lesson 2 to strengthen evidence-based reasoning?
5. Was the Wakulima Market context genuinely engaging for your learners, or did some learners seem disconnected from it? If disconnected, what local adaptation (a different Kenyan market, a different circular food) might create stronger personal relevance for your specific class?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed four watermelon-slice sectors — all with radius 7 cm but with central angles of 30°, 90°, 120°, and 180° — drawn on centimetre-square grid paper. By counting squares, they found that the estimated area increases as the central angle increases, and that Sector D (180°) has approximately twice the area of Sector B (90°), mirroring the doubling of the angle.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a sector-shaped piece of a circle is NOT fixed by the radius alone — it changes dramatically with the central angle. When the radius is the same, doubling the central angle approximately doubles the area. Two variables control the size of a watermelon slice: the radius (r) and the central angle (θ). Prior methods for finding area (rectangles, triangles) cannot handle the curved boundary of a sector.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This begins to explain why Mama Wanjiku's customers receive such different amounts of watermelon even though every piece was cut from the same melon: the vendor changed the angle of each cut, and because area is proportional to the central angle, a small change in angle produces a large difference in the amount of fruit. A 30° slice contains only one-sixth as much watermelon as the 180° slice, even though both pieces look 'like a slice' and share the same radius. The exact formula — which will be derived in Lesson 2 — is needed to calculate fair shares precisely.

slo.purpose: Learners derive the formula for the area of a sector by reasoning that a sector is a fraction of a full circle, then apply it to calculate the exact area of watermelon wedges at Wakulima Market.
slo.knowledge:
• A sector is a fraction of a full circle determined by the ratio of the central angle to 360°.
• The area of a sector = (θ/360°) × πr², where θ is the central angle in degrees and r is the radius.
• The two variables that determine sector area are the central angle (θ) and the radius (r); doubling either changes the area predictably.
slo.skills:
• Derive the sector area formula by reasoning from proportionality between central angle and full circle area.
• Calculate the area of a sector given the radius and central angle, expressing answers to 2 decimal places using π ≈ 3.142.
• Verify predictions from Lesson 1 by substituting values into the derived formula.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematical formulas are not arbitrary rules but logical conclusions derived from reasoning about proportions.
• Demonstrate persistence and collaborative spirit when working through derivation steps with peers.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners established that sector area depends on both radius and central angle. This lesson advances the storyline by giving learners the precise mathematical tool — the sector area formula — so they can calculate exactly how much watermelon is in each wedge and begin to resolve the fair-sharing dispute at Wakulima Market.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure compasses are handled carefully when drawing circles; remind learners to keep compass points directed downward when not in use.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the first formal evidence-gathering lesson in the sequence. Building directly on Lesson 1, where learners discovered that sector area is jointly controlled by radius and central angle, learners now derive the sector area formula through proportional reasoning. The central idea is elegantly simple: a sector is nothing more than a fraction of a full circle, and that fraction equals the ratio of the central angle to 360°. By treating the full circle as the reference unit, learners construct the formula themselves rather than receiving it passively.

The lesson opens with learners revisiting their Lesson 1 predictions about the 45°, 90°, and 135° watermelon wedges. The teacher uses a large paper circle (the same one from Lesson 1) and guides learners to express each sector as a fraction of the whole circle, then multiply by the full circle area (πr²). This proportional reasoning — naming the sensemaking strategy as "Fraction of a Whole" — is made visible by folding and overlaying cut-out sectors so learners can physically see that four 90° sectors reconstitute the full circle. Pairs then practise the formula on three worked examples set firmly in the Wakulima Market context, computing exact areas in cm² for wedges of known radii and angles.

By the end of the lesson, learners can calculate the precise area of any sector, compare their results to their Lesson 1 predictions, and articulate why Mama Achieng's differently-angled slices are genuinely unequal in area. This resolution of the opening puzzle is recorded on the Driving Question Board and feeds directly into the cumulative model learners are building across the eight-lesson sequence.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually re-examine the three sector diagrams from Lesson 1 (45°, 90°, and 135°, all with radius 14 cm drawn on the board). Each learner writes in their exercise book: (a) what fraction of the full circle they think each sector represents, and (b) a numerical estimate of each sector's area in cm², showing their working. After writing, pairs share and compare estimates, noting any disagreements.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three sector diagrams prominently and say: 'Before we derive any formula today, I want you to think like a mathematician. Look at these three watermelon slices from Mama Achieng's stall. In your book, write down: what fraction of the whole watermelon circle is each slice? Then estimate its area.' Allow 3 minutes of silent individual writing. After 3 minutes, say: 'Now turn to your partner and compare your fractions. Do you agree?' Allow 90 seconds of pair discussion. Cold-call 4 learners (select across the room — front-left, back-right, middle, and one who looks uncertain): 'Wanjiku, what fraction did you write for the 90° slice?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds minimum before prompting. Record all four responses on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — Lesson 2'. Do NOT confirm or reject any prediction yet. Say: 'Hold onto these predictions. By the end of today, you will know exactly who is right — and more importantly, why.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Anchored Prediction: Learners connect new reasoning (fractions) to the same phenomenon anchor used in Lesson 1. Writing predictions before instruction activates prior knowledge of fractions and primes learners to notice when the formula confirms or corrects their thinking, deepening retention.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans exercise books during pair discussion, looking for: (1) whether learners correctly express 90° as 1/4 of 360° — this reveals whether proportional reasoning about angles is accessible; (2) whether area estimates are in a reasonable range (e.g., 90° sector of r=14 cm should be near 154 cm²). Learners who write 'I don't know how to estimate' are flagged for targeted support during the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners participate in a structured paper-folding and cut-out investigation. Each pair receives a pre-cut paper circle of radius 14 cm and three pre-cut sector cut-outs: 45°, 90°, and 135°. Learners first fold the 90° sector in half and observe it is exactly 1/4 of the full circle. They then physically tile four 90° sectors onto the full circle to confirm 4 × 90° = 360°. Next, learners complete a guided observation table in their books with three columns: Central Angle (θ), Fraction of Full Circle (θ/360°), and 'What we multiplied the full circle area by'. They record observations for all three sectors. Finally, the teacher reveals the full circle area formula (A = πr²) and learners calculate the full circle area for r = 14 cm as a shared step.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the pre-cut materials and say: 'Your job is to be a detective. I want you to physically discover how a sector relates to the full circle. Start by placing your 90° sector on the full circle. How many times does it fit?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds. After learners respond, say: 'Write that down as a fraction. Now do the same for the 45° and 135° sectors — how many of each would fill the full circle?' Circulate actively, pausing at each pair for 20–30 seconds. Use probing questions: 'How did you get that fraction?', 'What does the 360 in the denominator represent?' After 6 minutes of hands-on work, bring the class together. Draw a table on the board and cold-call 3 learners to fill in the three rows of the fraction column. Then say: 'The full circle has area πr². For our watermelon with r = 14 cm, let's calculate that together.' Write on the board: A_circle = π × 14² = π × 196 ≈ 3.142 × 196 = 615.83 cm². Say: 'Now — if the full circle is 615.83 cm², and a 90° sector is one-quarter of the circle, what is the sector's area?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. Confirm the answer (≈ 153.96 cm²) and connect it back to the prediction board: 'Look at your prediction from the start of the lesson. How close were you?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Fraction of a Whole (Concrete-to-Abstract Bridge): Physically tiling sectors onto the full circle makes the proportional relationship tangible before any algebraic formula is introduced. This concrete manipulation prevents the formula from being received as an arbitrary rule and instead positions it as a description of something learners have already seen and touched — directly analogous to Mama Achieng's physical cutting of the watermelon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks the observation table during circulation. Key indicators: (1) Learners correctly write θ/360° for all three sectors (not θ/180° or θ/π — common errors); (2) Learners can explain in words why the denominator is 360°; (3) Learners who tile sectors correctly but cannot express it as a fraction need targeted support linking the physical action to the symbolic fraction. Record names of learners who are consistently inaccurate for follow-up in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners formalise the derivation in their books. Working individually, each learner writes out the full derivation in three steps: Step 1 — express the sector as a fraction of the circle (θ/360°); Step 2 — the full circle area is πr²; Step 3 — therefore, Area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr². Learners then apply the formula to three graded practice problems, all set in the Wakulima Market context: (A) a 60° slice of radius 21 cm (a mango segment at a nearby stall), (B) a 120° slice of radius 10.5 cm (a pawpaw wedge), and (C) Mama Achieng's three original watermelon slices — 45°, 90°, and 135° at r = 14 cm — for which they now calculate exact areas and compare with their Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 predictions.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We are now going to capture what we discovered as a formula. Write this heading in your book: Derivation of the Sector Area Formula.' Guide learners step-by-step, writing each line on the board and pausing for learners to copy and annotate: 'A sector with central angle θ is (θ/360°) of the full circle. The full circle has area πr². Therefore: Area of sector = (θ/360°) × πr².' Say: 'Box this formula. Every time you use it, you should be able to explain where it came from — from the paper circle we just folded.' Assign the three practice problems. Say: 'Work individually and silently for 5 minutes. Show all three steps for each problem.' After 5 minutes, cold-call 3 different learners (one per problem) to write their solutions on the board. For each solution ask the class: 'Do you agree with this answer? Give a thumbs up if you got the same, thumbs sideways if slightly different, thumbs down if very different.' Address any thumbs-down responses immediately with targeted re-teaching. For Problem C, say: 'Now compare your exact answers with the predictions you wrote in Lesson 1. What do you notice? Has anything surprised you?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Guided Derivation with Annotated Formula: Rather than stating the formula and practising it, learners write the derivation in their own books with annotations explaining each line. This metacognitive narration strategy (writing 'because the sector is a fraction of the whole circle' next to the formula) ensures the formula is stored with meaning attached, not as an isolated rule. Connecting back to the three specific Wakulima Market slices grounds abstract algebra in the concrete phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects answers to Problem C as a key formative checkpoint. Correct answers: 45° sector ≈ 76.99 cm²; 90° sector ≈ 153.99 cm²; 135° sector ≈ 230.98 cm². Learners who obtain these answers (±0.5 cm² rounding tolerance) have met the lesson SLO. Common errors to watch for: (1) using diameter instead of radius; (2) writing (θ/180°) instead of (θ/360°); (3) forgetting to square the radius. Any learner making error (2) or (3) on more than one problem is flagged for re-teaching before Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (established in Lesson 1). Each learner writes one sticky note (or index card) responding to the prompt: 'What can I now calculate that I couldn't calculate before this lesson?' They also annotate the three prediction cards from Lesson 1 with the actual computed values (in a different colour) so the board shows both prediction and evidence side by side. Two volunteers read their sticky notes aloud before they are posted.
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners' attention to the DQB: 'Look at the predictions we recorded at the start of Lesson 1 and today. We now have exact numbers. Take your index card and write: what new calculating power do you have today that you didn't have after Lesson 1?' Allow 2 minutes of individual writing. Invite 2 volunteers to read their cards aloud before posting. Then point to the driving question displayed at the top of the DQB: 'How can we calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped piece of a circle so that every customer at Wakulima Market gets a fair share?' Say: 'Can we answer this question for sectors now?' Elicit a brief class response. Then say: 'But look — Mama Achieng's watermelon also has a curved rind and some slices are cut all the way through. What if the piece is not a full wedge but a shape bounded by a chord rather than two radii? Write one question on the board that this new knowledge makes you wonder about.' Collect 2–3 student-generated questions and post them on the DQB under the heading 'New Questions from Lesson 2'. These will anchor Lesson 3 (area of a segment).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence Layering on the DQB: By writing actual computed values next to earlier predictions in a contrasting colour, the DQB becomes a visible record of the class's growing precision. The shift from 'I estimated about 150 cm²' to 'I can now calculate exactly 153.99 cm²' is captured publicly, reinforcing the epistemic value of deriving and applying a formula. Student-generated questions on the board sustain curiosity and create authentic need for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads the sticky notes as they are posted. A well-formed response names the formula (e.g., 'I can now use Area = (θ/360°) × πr² to calculate the exact area of any sector') and connects it to the phenomenon (e.g., 'so I can tell Mama Achieng's customers exactly how many cm² are in their slice'). Vague responses such as 'I learned about circles' indicate surface-level engagement and require a follow-up oral probe: 'Can you show me with an example?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update their cumulative visual model of a watermelon cross-section, which was started in Lesson 1. In Lesson 1, the model showed a circle with three sectors labelled with angles and arrows indicating 'bigger angle = bigger area'. In this lesson, learners add: (1) the sector area formula written inside one of the sectors; (2) exact area values (in cm²) labelled on each of the three sectors (45° ≈ 76.99 cm², 90° ≈ 153.99 cm², 135° ≈ 230.98 cm²); (3) a ratio note showing that the 135° slice is exactly 3× the area of the 45° slice, reinforcing proportionality. Learners write one sentence beneath the model: 'Mama Achieng's slices are NOT equal — the 135° slice has 3 times more watermelon than the 45° slice.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open to your model from Lesson 1. Today we are going to make it more precise. Add the formula, the exact areas, and the ratio relationship we discovered.' Display a reference diagram on the board showing where each annotation should go. Circulate for 3 minutes, checking that: (1) the formula is written correctly (not from memory error); (2) the ratio 3:1 is correctly identified (135°/45° = 3). As learners finish, cold-call 1 learner to hold up their model and explain one annotation to the class in one sentence. Say: 'Your model is now a mathematical argument. If Mama Achieng's customer challenged you, you could use this diagram to prove that the 135° slice is three times larger than the 45° slice.' Finally, preview the next lesson: 'Next time, we will look at a different kind of slice — one where the cut is straight across, like a chord, not two radii. This is called a segment. Does your formula still work? That is our next puzzle.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: The model serves as a running scientific and mathematical argument that grows in precision across lessons. Each revision adds a layer of evidence (qualitative in Lesson 1, quantitative in Lesson 2) without erasing earlier thinking, so learners can trace their own conceptual development. Labelling exact values and ratios directly on the watermelon cross-section keeps the abstract formula anchored to the real-world phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks models for three specific features: (1) formula written correctly as (θ/360°) × πr²; (2) at least two of the three sector areas labelled correctly (within ±1 cm² rounding); (3) a sentence or annotation that correctly connects formula output to the fairness question. Models missing the ratio annotation are flagged — this indicates the learner can compute but has not yet connected calculation to proportional reasoning, which is needed for Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Observe Phase, did all pairs correctly tile the 90° sector four times onto the full circle and express this as the fraction 1/4? If several pairs wrote 1/2 or 2/4 without simplifying, how will I address fraction simplification before Lesson 3 without derailing the sector content?
2. In the Explain Phase, which of the three common errors (using diameter, using 180° denominator, or forgetting to square r) appeared most frequently in learners' Problem C solutions? What targeted re-teaching micro-moment can I build into the opening 3 minutes of Lesson 3?
3. Did the sticky notes on the DQB show genuine connection to the phenomenon (mentioning Mama Achieng, Wakulima Market, fair shares), or were they generic mathematical statements? How can I use the phenomenon more explicitly in my questioning next lesson?
4. Were the student-generated questions posted at the end of the DQB phase pointing naturally toward segments, or did learners raise other ideas (e.g., arc length, volume of the watermelon)? How will I honour and sequence those questions in the remaining lessons?
5. When cold-calling during the Predict Phase, did I genuinely wait at least 12 seconds, or did I prompt too early? Review my timing — was there equitable cold-calling across gender and seating zones in the classroom?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners physically tiled pre-cut sector cut-outs onto a full paper circle of radius 14 cm and observed that four 90° sectors, eight 45° sectors, or approximately 2.67 of the 135° sectors reconstitute the full circle — confirming that each sector is a measurable fraction (θ/360°) of the whole.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a sector equals the fraction of the full circle it occupies multiplied by the full circle area: Area = (θ/360°) × πr². For Mama Achieng's watermelon (r = 14 cm), the 45° slice ≈ 76.99 cm², the 90° slice ≈ 153.99 cm², and the 135° slice ≈ 230.98 cm² — confirming that the 135° slice is exactly three times larger than the 45° slice.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The fair-sharing dispute at Wakulima Market can now be resolved mathematically: Mama Achieng's slices are provably unequal because they have different central angles. The sector area formula gives every customer an objective tool to verify the size of their slice in cm², directly answering the driving question for wedge-shaped pieces. The remaining puzzle is whether the same approach works for a segment (a slice bounded by a straight chord rather than two radii).

LESSONS.title: Investigating Sector Area with Cut-Outs
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle

slo.purpose: Learners derive and apply the formula for the area of a sector by physically constructing, measuring, and comparing paper cut-out sectors of different radii and angles — directly connecting their findings to the watermelon-slice phenomenon at Wakulima Market.
slo.knowledge: Learners determine that the area of a sector of a circle is given by A = (θ/360) × πr², where θ is the angle subtended at the centre and r is the radius, and that changing either variable changes the area proportionally.
slo.skills: Learners measure radius and central angle of paper cut-out sectors, calculate sector areas using the derived formula, compare results across different sectors, and communicate mathematical reasoning to peers.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that precise mathematical formulas enable fair and accurate measurement of curved shapes, and demonstrate Unity and Peace by collaborating respectfully when constructing cut-outs and sharing findings.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 2 (OBSERVE), learners gathered qualitative evidence — they saw that different central angles produce visually different wedge sizes. In Lesson 3 they move from observation to quantification: they construct their own sector cut-outs, measure them, and derive the sector-area formula. This gives them the first precise mathematical tool for answering the driving question — calculating exactly how many cm² of watermelon are in any given wedge, so that Mama Akinyi at Wakulima Market can price and cut fairly.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use scissors and compasses during cut-out construction. Remind learners to handle scissors with blades pointing downward and to place compasses on the desk when not in use. No running with sharp instruments.

LESSONS.overview: Learners construct paper cut-outs of sectors with varying central angles (30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) and a fixed radius, then with varying radii and a fixed angle. They measure, record, and calculate areas, ultimately deriving A = (θ/360) × πr² from the pattern in their data. They then test the formula against the watermelon-slice phenomenon by calculating the area of two specific vendor cuts described in the anchoring scenario and determining whether the vendor's cuts are truly fair. The lesson bridges the qualitative evidence from Lesson 2 to the quantitative toolkit needed for Lessons 4–8.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-page printed sheet showing five sector outlines: all with radius 7 cm but central angles of 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, and 180°. Without any formula, learners individually write two predictions in their exercise books: (1) 'I predict the sector with angle 180° has ___ times the area of the sector with angle 90°, because…' and (2) 'If I double the radius but keep the angle fixed, I predict the area will ___.' Learners then compare predictions with a desk partner for 2 minutes before a whole-class share-out.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the printed sector-outline sheet. Say: 'Before we calculate anything today, I want you to THINK about what you already believe. Look at these five watermelon slices — same melon, same radius, different cuts. In your book, complete both prediction sentences. You have 3 minutes of silent thinking time — GO.' Set a visible 3-minute timer. After 3 minutes say: 'Turn to your desk partner — compare your predictions. Do you agree? If not, why not? You have 2 minutes.' After partner talk, cold-call 3 learners (one who predicted a doubling relationship, one who did not, one who is unsure) using: 'Kamau — share your prediction for question 1 and your reasoning.' Apply 10-second wait time after each cold-call before accepting any response. Record two or three contrasting predictions visibly on the board under the heading 'OUR PREDICTIONS — we will test these today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-then-Test anchoring: By committing predictions to writing before any instruction, learners activate prior knowledge about proportionality and area, create cognitive dissonance that motivates the activity, and have a personal benchmark against which to evaluate their later findings. This directly mirrors the market vendor's implicit prediction that equal angles mean equal area.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate during silent writing. Look for: (a) learners who correctly predict a proportional (linear) relationship between angle and area — this shows strong proportional reasoning; (b) learners who predict the radius relationship will also be linear (rather than quadratic) — this is the key misconception to address in Phase 3. Note names of both groups for targeted questioning in Phase 3. Observable indicator: every learner has at least one written prediction sentence before partner talk begins.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive a Materials Pack: one sheet of A4 card, a compass, protractor, ruler, scissors, and a recording table (pre-printed or copied from the board). PART A — Fixed radius, varying angle (15 min): Each group draws and cuts out 5 sectors on card, all with radius 7 cm, at angles 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°. For each sector they measure the arc length with a string-and-ruler method, record the central angle θ and radius r, and calculate the fraction θ/360. They record these in their table. PART B — Fixed angle, varying radius (8 min): Groups draw and cut out 3 sectors all at 60°, with radii 4 cm, 7 cm, and 10 cm. They record r, r², and the fraction θ/360 for each. PART C — Pattern hunt (5 min): Groups inspect their two tables and write one sentence describing the pattern they see between (θ/360) and area, and another sentence describing the relationship between r and area.
framework.teacherMoves: Before groups begin say: 'You are now Mama Akinyi's quality-control team. She needs to know the exact area of each wedge — not an estimate, the EXACT area. Your cut-outs are your evidence. Every measurement must be recorded in your table — a scientist at KEMRI would not skip a row.' Circulate continuously. At the 7-minute mark, pause the class for a 60-second mid-activity check: cold-call one group — 'Group 3 — Aisha, tell me: what is θ/360 for your 90° sector?' (10-second wait time). If the group says 0.25, affirm and say: 'Hold that number — it will matter in Phase 3.' If incorrect, prompt: 'What fraction of the full 360° is 90°?' For Part B, prompt groups who finish early: 'Look at your r column and your area column. What happens to the area when r doubles from 4 to 8? Is that what you predicted?' During Part C, circulate and listen for the word 'proportional' — if no group uses it, plant the seed: 'Is the relationship between θ and area the same KIND of relationship as between r and area? Discuss.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-Table Pattern Recognition with Physical Manipulatives: Learners generate their own data through measurement of self-constructed objects, rather than reading values from a textbook. The physical act of cutting sectors at different angles makes the proportional relationship between angle and area visceral and memorable. Separating the two variables (Part A then Part B) follows a controlled-variable investigation structure (NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 3: Planning and Carrying Out Investigations), enabling learners to isolate the effect of each variable on area.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect observable evidence at three checkpoints: (1) At 10 minutes — every group should have at least 3 completed rows in their Part A table with θ/360 correctly calculated; (2) At 20 minutes — Part B table should show r² values calculated, not just r; (3) At 28 minutes — each group's Part C pattern sentence should mention both angle and radius. Key misconception to watch: groups who calculate θ/360 × r (instead of θ/360 × r²) in Part C — flag these groups for direct questioning in Phase 3. Indicator of success: 100% of groups have a completed two-part data table with at least one pattern sentence written.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole-class discussion leads to derivation of the sector area formula. Learners then apply the formula to two specific cuts: Cut A (θ = 45°, r = 14 cm) and Cut B (θ = 72°, r = 14 cm) — the two wedges the Wakulima Market vendor claimed were 'fair.' Learners calculate both areas, compare them, and write a one-sentence verdict: 'The vendor's cuts ARE / ARE NOT fair because…' They also revisit their Phase 1 predictions and annotate them with 'CONFIRMED' or 'REVISED — because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Open with: 'Let's build the formula TOGETHER from YOUR data. I am not going to tell you the formula — you are going to derive it.' Draw a blank formula template on the board: Area of sector = ___ × Area of full circle. Ask cold-call question (10-second wait): 'Juma — from your Part A table, what fraction of the full circle is a 60° sector?' After response, fill in: 'So Area of 60° sector = (60/360) × πr².' Ask: 'Wanjiku — generalise that. If the angle is θ, what is the formula?' (10-second wait). Write A = (θ/360) × πr² on the board. Then ask: 'From your Part B data — when you DOUBLED the radius, what happened to the area?' Cold-call a third learner (10-second wait). Establish that area quadruples, confirming the r² term. Now pivot to the phenomenon: 'Mama Akinyi cuts two slices: one at 45°, one at 72°, both from a melon of radius 14 cm. Use the formula — calculate both areas in your book. You have 4 minutes.' After 4 minutes, cold-call two learners to share answers and write them on the board. Ask: 'Is that a fair price if she charges the same for both? What would YOU tell her?' End Phase 3 by directing learners back to their Phase 1 prediction page: 'Annotate your predictions — were you right? Write CONFIRMED or REVISED and explain why in one sentence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Guided Derivation with Phenomenon Application (NGSS SEP 6 — Constructing Explanations): Rather than presenting the formula as a given fact, the teacher scaffolds learners to construct it from their own data, then immediately apply it to the anchoring phenomenon. This two-step move — derive, then deploy — ensures the formula is understood as an explanation of the physical reality of the watermelon slices, not an abstract rule. Connecting back to the vendor scenario embeds the mathematics in a justice and fairness context meaningful to Kenyan learners.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect exercise books during the 4-minute calculation window and scan 4–5 books for: (a) correct substitution of θ = 45 and r = 14 into A = (θ/360) × πr²; (b) correct arithmetic (area of Cut A ≈ 76.97 cm²; area of Cut B ≈ 123.15 cm²); (c) a written verdict sentence. Misconception alert: learners who write A = (θ/360) × 2πr (using circumference formula instead of area formula) — address immediately by asking: 'Is πr² the area or the circumference of the full circle?' Observable indicator of meeting expectations: at least 80% of learners produce a correct numerical answer for both cuts and a verdict sentence before the phase ends.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives two sticky notes. On the GREEN note they write one thing they can NOW answer about the driving question that they could not answer before this lesson (e.g., 'I can now calculate the exact area of any wedge if I know r and θ'). On the ORANGE note they write one new question this lesson has raised (e.g., 'What if the watermelon slice is not a full wedge — what if it has a flat chord cut across the bottom?'). Learners post notes on the class DQB, which is organised into columns: WHAT WE PREDICTED, WHAT WE OBSERVED, WHAT WE CAN NOW EXPLAIN, WHAT WE STILL WONDER. The teacher reads three orange notes aloud and tells the class which upcoming lesson will address each question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our Driving Question is: how can we calculate the exact area of any wedge or segment-shaped piece of a circle? Look at the DQB. In Lesson 2 we filled the OBSERVED column. Today we fill WHAT WE CAN NOW EXPLAIN.' Hand out sticky notes. Allow 3 minutes of silent writing. As learners post notes, read three orange notes aloud — select at least one that anticipates the segment (chord-cut) concept. Say: 'This question — about a flat-bottom slice — is EXACTLY what Lesson 5 will answer. Keep wondering.' Point to the OBSERVED column from Lesson 2 and say: 'Notice how our observation that a bigger angle means a bigger piece is now backed by a formula. That is the power of mathematics — we moved from seeing to calculating.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board as Cumulative Sense-Making Record (NGSS SEP 8 — Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information): The DQB makes the progression of understanding visible across the eight-lesson sequence. Separating 'can now explain' from 'still wonder' trains learners to distinguish between resolved and unresolved questions — a core scientific literacy skill. The orange notes also provide the teacher with formative data on which concepts need pre-teaching before Lesson 5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect and read all orange sticky notes after class. Categorise them into: (a) segment vs. sector confusion — indicates readiness for Lesson 5; (b) radius-effect questions — indicates the r² relationship needs reinforcement in Lesson 4; (c) real-life application questions — indicates high engagement and readiness for design tasks in Lesson 7. Observable indicator: every learner posts both a green and an orange note.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative annotated diagram — a labelled drawing of a circular watermelon cross-section they began in Lesson 1 and annotated in Lesson 2. Today they add three new elements: (1) they label a sector with the formula A = (θ/360) × πr² written directly on the wedge; (2) they annotate one wedge with a worked numerical example using the Wakulima Market values (θ = 45°, r = 14 cm → A ≈ 76.97 cm²); (3) they draw an arrow from the formula to a speech bubble containing the text: 'This is why the vendor's 45° and 72° slices are NOT equal even though the radius is the same.' Learners write a one-line 'Model Update Statement' at the bottom of their diagram: 'I used to think the size of a wedge depended only on how it looked. Now I think it depends on BOTH the angle θ and the radius r, because A = (θ/360) × πr².'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out your cumulative watermelon diagram. You have been building this model since Lesson 1. Today you have a new, powerful piece of evidence to add — the formula. Add all three annotations I have written on the board.' Write the three annotation instructions on the board for reference. Circulate and look for learners who write the formula incorrectly (e.g., missing the r² or writing r instead of r²). Ask targeted questions: 'Chebet — in your formula, why is it r-squared and not just r? What did your Part B data tell you?' (10-second wait). In the final 2 minutes, cold-call one learner to read their Model Update Statement aloud. Ask the class: 'Does everyone agree with that statement? Give me a thumbs up if your statement says something similar.' Use thumbs to gauge class-wide consolidation before dismissal.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (NGSS SEP 2 — Developing and Using Models): The annotated diagram serves as a running scientific model that learners revise with each new lesson. Adding the formula directly onto the watermelon diagram — rather than into a separate notes section — reinforces that the formula is an explanation of the physical phenomenon, not an abstract mathematical object. The 'I used to think / Now I think' frame (adapted from Project Zero's Thinking Routine) makes conceptual change explicit and self-directed.
framework.formativeAssessment: At the end of class, collect 8 cumulative diagrams (2 per group) for a rapid check. Look for: (a) formula written correctly with both θ and r² present; (b) a worked numerical example with correct substitution; (c) a Model Update Statement that references BOTH variables. Learners whose diagrams are missing any element receive a written prompt sticker: 'What does your Part B data tell you about what happens to area when r changes?' to guide self-correction before Lesson 4. Observable indicator of meeting expectations: formula is correctly written on the diagram with at least one annotated numerical example.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your professional journal:
1. FORMULA DERIVATION: Did learners genuinely derive A = (θ/360) × πr² from their own data, or did they copy it from the board? In your next lesson, ask two or three learners to explain in their own words why the formula contains r² — their explanations will reveal the depth of conceptual understanding.
2. THE r² MISCONCEPTION: How many learners initially wrote r instead of r² in their formula? This is the most common error in this sub-strand. If more than 30% of the class made this error, open Lesson 4 with a brief re-engagement with the Part B data: 'When Amina's radius went from 4 cm to 8 cm (doubled), what happened to the area?' Use their own recorded data to self-correct.
3. FAIR-SHARING VERDICT: Did learners engage with the justice dimension of the vendor scenario — that unequal cut angles produce unfair portions? Or did they treat it as a purely computational exercise? If the fairness angle was missed, find a moment in Lesson 4 to ask: 'What would you charge per cm² for a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market if the whole melon costs KSh 150?'
4. DQB ORANGE NOTES: Review the orange sticky notes tonight. If most questions are about segments (flat-bottom slices), learners are ahead of pace and you can briefly preview the chord-cut concept at the start of Lesson 4. If questions are still about sectors, consolidate before moving forward.
5. GROUP DYNAMICS: Did all learners in each group of 4 physically handle the compass and scissors, or did one learner dominate the construction? For Lesson 4, assign roles explicitly: Compass Operator, Protractor Reader, Recorder, and Reporter — rotating roles ensures equitable participation and richer individual learning.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners constructed paper cut-out sectors of a circle with varying central angles (30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) at a fixed radius of 7 cm, and sectors at a fixed angle of 60° with varying radii (4 cm, 7 cm, 10 cm). They measured, recorded data in tables, and identified patterns — that area scales linearly with central angle and as the square of the radius.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a sector of a circle is given by A = (θ/360) × πr², where θ is the central angle in degrees and r is the radius. Doubling the angle doubles the area; doubling the radius quadruples the area. Learners applied this formula to calculate the areas of two Wakulima Market watermelon wedges (θ = 45° and θ = 72°, r = 14 cm) and determined the vendor's equal-price claim was mathematically unfair.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The sector area formula is derived from the fact that a sector is a fraction (θ/360) of the full circle. Because the full circle has area πr², any sector has area (θ/360) × πr². This explains why the vendor's two wedge-cuts at different angles produce measurably different areas even though both come from the same melon — changing only the angle of the cut directly and proportionally changes the area of the piece.
