LESSONS.title: Cutting Watermelon Fairly: Deriving the Area of a Sector Formula
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle

slo.purpose: Learners derive and apply the formula for the area of a sector by physically cutting out sectors of different angles from printed circles, tabulating results, and identifying the proportional relationship between angle size and area.
slo.knowledge: The area of a sector of a circle is a fraction of the total circle area, given by Area = (θ/360) × πr², where θ is the central angle in degrees and r is the radius.
slo.skills: Learners measure angles and radii using a protractor and ruler, calculate sector areas as fractions of the full circle area, tabulate data, and identify a mathematical pattern from evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics provides an exact, fair method for comparing and calculating wedge-shaped portions — resolving real disputes like those at Wakulima Market — and value precision and collaborative inquiry.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3, learners established that the angle of a wedge cut changes the size of a watermelon slice, estimated sizes qualitatively, and reviewed the formula for the area of a full circle (πr²). In Lesson 4 — the core evidence-gathering lesson — learners move from estimation to exact calculation: they physically construct sectors of five different angles, measure them, compute each area as a fraction of πr², and discover the general formula Area = (θ/360) × πr². This formula is the quantitative tool needed to answer the driving question and resolve the Wakulima Market fairness dispute.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners will use scissors to cut printed circles. Remind all learners to cut away from their bodies and neighbouring learners. Collect and store scissors immediately after the cutting phase. Learners with any hand injury should measure and record rather than cut.

LESSONS.overview: Learners work in groups of 4. Each group receives a printed circle of radius 7 cm, a protractor, scissors, a ruler, and a recording table. Groups mark and cut out sectors of 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, and 180° from their circles. They arrange the sectors side by side, observe the dramatic size differences, measure each sector's angle and radius, then calculate the area of each sector as a fraction of the full circle area (πr² = 154 cm²). Results are tabulated across the whole class and the pattern — Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr² — is surfaced through structured questioning. The lesson ends with groups writing the formula in their own words and applying it to two new sector problems set in a Kenyan context (a slice of ugali cake and a door-sweep in Kisumu). Every step is anchored to the Wakulima Market watermelon phenomenon: learners are calculating exactly how much watermelon is in each wedge.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group is shown a circle drawn on the board (radius 7 cm) with five sectors marked: 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°. Without calculating, learners individually write two predictions in their exercise books: (1) 'If the full circle area is 154 cm², what do you estimate the area of the 90° sector is?' and (2) 'Which two sectors together would give exactly half the circle?' Learners share predictions with their group partner for 1 minute, then the teacher cold-calls 3 learners to share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Draw the five-sector circle on the board clearly, labelling each angle. Say: 'Before we cut anything, I want your best guess. Look at the full circle — its area is 154 cm². In your exercise book, write your estimate for the area of the 90° sector and explain your reasoning.' WAIT TIME: 30 seconds of silent thinking. Then say: 'Share your prediction with your partner. You have 1 minute.' After 1 minute, cold-call 3 learners by name: 'Amina, what did you predict and why? … Brian, do you agree with Amina? … Zawadi, what was different about your thinking?' Record the range of predictions on the board without correcting them — label it 'OUR PREDICTIONS'. Say: 'We will come back to check these predictions against our evidence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-observe (anticipation guide): By committing to a numerical estimate before gathering data, learners activate prior knowledge of fractions and circle area, and create a cognitive need to test their predictions. Recording predictions publicly creates accountability and makes conceptual change visible later.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen for whether learners use proportional reasoning (e.g., '90° is a quarter of 360° so the area should be a quarter of 154') versus additive or visual guessing. Cold-call responses reveal whether the fraction-of-a-whole concept is accessible. If fewer than 2 of 3 cold-called learners use any fractional reasoning, pause and ask the whole class: 'What fraction of a full turn is 90°?' before proceeding.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives: one printed circle (radius = 7 cm, with 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180° sectors pre-marked), scissors, a protractor, a ruler, and a group recording table (columns: Angle θ, Radius r, Full circle area πr², Fraction θ/360, Calculated area). Groups cut out each sector carefully, arrange the five cut-outs side by side on their desk in order from smallest to largest, and then fill in columns 1–3 of the table by measuring the angle (confirm with protractor) and radius of each sector. They also compute πr² = π × 7² ≈ 154 cm² together as a group before proceeding to column 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and say: 'Each group, cut out your five sectors carefully — scissors away from your body. Once cut, line them up on your desk from the smallest angle to the largest. What do you notice just by looking?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds after groups line up sectors, then cold-call 2 groups: 'Group Kisumu, describe what you see. … Group Mombasa, does your arrangement look the same?' Then direct: 'Now measure the angle of each cut-out with your protractor to confirm it, and measure the radius with your ruler. Record these in columns 1 and 2 of your table.' Circulate. At each group, ask: 'What is the full circle area for a circle of radius 7 cm? Show me how you worked it out.' WAIT TIME: 20 seconds before prompting if needed. If a group is stuck, say: 'What is the formula for the area of a full circle?' — not the answer. Ensure every group writes πr² = π × 49 ≈ 154 cm² in column 3 before moving on. After 8 minutes, pause the class and say: 'Hold up your five cut-outs. Class — look at the 30° sector and the 180° sector side by side. The vendor at Wakulima Market says these two slices are equally fair. Is she right? We need numbers, not just eyes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Physical manipulation and data collection (Concrete–Representational–Abstract progression): Cutting and arranging physical sectors grounds the abstract formula in tangible objects. The five cut-outs on the desk become a concrete data set that learners can see, touch, and compare before any algebraic generalisation is made. Measuring to confirm pre-marked angles reinforces the meaning of central angle.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate and check two specific observable indicators: (1) Every group can state and write πr² = 154 cm² correctly before moving to column 4 — if not, the formula for full circle area is not secure and must be addressed immediately. (2) When groups arrange sectors, check they place them in ascending order of angle (30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°) — this shows they understand angle determines size. If any group places sectors randomly, ask: 'Which sector has the smallest angle? Place that one first.'

framework.learnerExperience: Groups complete columns 4 and 5 of their recording table: for each sector, they calculate the fraction θ/360 and then multiply by 154 cm² to find the sector area. They record results neatly in the table. A class data-sharing moment follows: the teacher builds a shared class table on the board as each group calls out their results. Learners look for the pattern across the five rows and write a sentence in their books: 'The area of a sector = ___.' Groups then apply the formula to two new problems: (A) A circular ugali cake of radius 14 cm is cut into a 45° slice for a guest — what is the area of the slice? (B) When a door in a Kisumu office opens 120°, it sweeps a sector of radius 80 cm on the floor — what area of floor does it sweep?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Now complete columns 4 and 5. For column 4, divide your angle by 360. For column 5, multiply that fraction by 154. You have 5 minutes.' Circulate and, at each group, ask: 'For your 90° sector — what fraction of the full circle is it? … So what is its area?' WAIT TIME: 30 seconds per question. Cold-call the answer from the group, not just the nearest learner. After 5 minutes, build the class table on the board by cold-calling each group for one row: 'Group Nairobi, give me the row for 60°.' Fill the table. Then ask the whole class: 'Look at the five rows. What pattern do you see between the angle and the area?' WAIT TIME: 30 seconds of silent individual thinking, then pair-share for 1 minute. Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Kendi and Otieno, what pattern did you find?' Guide toward: 'Area = (θ/360) × πr².' Write this on the board and say: 'Write this formula in your own words as a sentence in your exercise book.' Then present problems A and B: 'The mama mboga has a new problem. A customer wants the 45° ugali-cake slice — exactly how much ugali in cm² does she get? And a Kisumu office needs to know how much floor space the door sweeps. Use our formula.' Groups work for 5 minutes; cold-call one group per problem to present their working on the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern recognition from a class data table (Data-driven generalisation): By pooling all five data points into a single shared table, learners see the linear relationship between θ and area across the full range 30°–180°. Writing the formula as a sentence before using it algebraically ensures conceptual ownership rather than rote copying. Applying the formula to two new Kenyan contexts (ugali cake, office door) immediately tests transfer and connects to the driving question's real-life dimension.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check two things during the apply phase: (1) Both problems must show the substitution step written out (e.g., Area = (45/360) × π × 14²) — if a group writes only the final answer, ask: 'Show me every step.' (2) Listen for whether learners simplify 45/360 to 1/8 correctly. A common error is treating θ/360 as θ × 360 — if this appears, draw the class's attention to it: 'What fraction of a pizza is one slice if you cut it into 8 equal pieces?' Use this as a whole-class re-teaching moment if more than 1 group makes this error.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives two sticky notes (or writes on the class DQB section of the board). On the first sticky note (GREEN), they write one thing they can now answer about the driving question: 'We can now calculate the area of any sector if we know r and θ.' On the second sticky note (ORANGE), they write one new question or remaining puzzle that the lesson raised — for example: 'But what about the curved segment below a chord? That's not the same as a sector.' The teacher reads selected notes aloud and organises them on the DQB under columns: 'What we have figured out' and 'What we still need to figure out.'
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners to the DQB. Say: 'We have been building our answer to the big question about Wakulima Market. On your green note, write one specific thing you can NOW calculate that you couldn't at the start of Lesson 1. Be precise — use the word formula or the word fraction.' WAIT TIME: 45 seconds of silent writing. Then: 'On your orange note, write one thing that our formula still cannot solve — think about the watermelon rind shape that is left over after you remove the triangular part of the slice.' WAIT TIME: 30 seconds. Cold-call 2 green notes and 2 orange notes. Post them on the DQB. Say: 'Notice that several groups are asking about segments — the region between a chord and an arc. That is exactly what we investigate in Lesson 5. We are building our answer piece by piece, just like the mama mboga builds her price by piece.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board update (metacognitive progress tracking): The two-colour sticky note protocol makes learners' growing understanding visible and public. Distinguishing 'figured out' from 'still need to figure out' mirrors scientific practice — no single lesson answers everything. The teacher's act of reading and categorising notes models how scientists track the state of their knowledge and identify the next investigative step.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read the green notes for specificity — acceptable notes reference the formula Area = (θ/360) × πr² or a specific calculation. Vague notes like 'we learned about sectors' indicate surface engagement. If more than half the green notes are vague, ask the class: 'Can someone give me a green note that includes a number or a formula?' — prompt revision before posting. Orange notes that mention segments or chords confirm readiness for Lesson 5 and can be highlighted as the bridge.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the annotated diagram of the Wakulima Market watermelon they began building in Lesson 1 (or draw a fresh circle of radius 7 cm if it is their first model). They now add three new annotations: (1) Label any two sectors on their diagram with their angle and calculated area (e.g., '90° sector → Area = 38.5 cm²'). (2) Write the general formula Area = (θ/360) × πr² inside or beside the circle. (3) Draw an arrow from the formula to the phenomenon caption and write: 'This formula tells the mama mboga exactly how much watermelon (in cm²) any wedge contains — so every customer can be charged fairly by area, not by eye.' Groups share their updated model with the group next to them and give one piece of feedback using the sentence stem: 'Your model clearly shows ___, and it could be improved by ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model diagram from Lesson 1. We are going to update it with today's evidence. You have 4 minutes to add three things — I am putting them on the board.' Write on the board: '1. Label 2 sectors with angle AND area. 2. Write the formula Area = (θ/360) × πr². 3. Write one sentence connecting the formula to the mama mboga's problem.' Circulate and, for each group, ask: 'Read me your sentence connecting the formula to the market. Does it answer the driving question?' WAIT TIME: 20 seconds after each prompt. After 4 minutes, say: 'Swap your model with the group next to you. Use this sentence: Your model clearly shows ___, and it could be improved by ___. You have 2 minutes.' Cold-call 1 group to share the feedback they received. Close by saying: 'Our model is growing. Today we added the exact formula. In Lesson 5 we will add segments — the curved sliver of rind — and our model will be even more powerful.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative annotated model revision (progressive model building): Returning to the same diagram across lessons externalises conceptual growth — learners can literally see what they have added each lesson. The peer feedback protocol using a structured sentence stem introduces scientific peer review norms and ensures models are evaluated against the driving question, not just aesthetics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect or photograph 2–3 group models. Check: (1) Formula is written correctly — Area = (θ/360) × πr², not a variant like Area = θ/360 × r. (2) The two labelled sectors show correct numerical areas (e.g., 90° → 38.5 cm², 60° → 25.67 cm²). (3) The connecting sentence explicitly mentions 'fair', 'area', or 'customer' — indicating the learner is connecting the mathematics to the phenomenon, not treating it as an abstract exercise. Use model photographs as evidence for portfolio assessment.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Did all five groups successfully derive Area = (θ/360) × πr² from their data, or did some groups need the formula supplied? If more than 2 groups could not identify the pattern independently, consider whether the recording table needs a hint column (e.g., a pre-filled row for 180° showing 180/360 = 1/2) in future. (2) Were learners able to transfer the formula to the ugali cake and door-sweep problems? If transfer was weak, the apply phase needs a worked example before independent group practice. (3) Did the DQB orange notes mention segments? If not, learners may not yet be distinguishing sectors from segments — this distinction must be made explicit at the start of Lesson 5 before moving to the segment formula. (4) Were scissors managed safely? Note any group that needed additional safety reminders for the school's records. (5) Review the 2–3 collected model diagrams: are the phenomenon connections in the sentence annotations genuine, or are they formulaic? Genuine connections (mentioning fairness, price, or customer) indicate the phenomenon is driving the learning effectively.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners cut out five sectors of angles 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°, and 180° from a printed circle of radius 7 cm, arranged them in order, measured their angles and radii, and recorded the full circle area (πr² ≈ 154 cm²) as the baseline.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a sector is a fraction of the full circle area determined by the central angle: Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². A 90° sector contains exactly one quarter of the full circle area; a 180° sector contains exactly half. Changing only the angle — while keeping the radius constant — changes the area proportionally.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners applied the formula to two new Kenyan contexts (a 45° ugali cake slice with r = 14 cm, and a door sweep of 120° with r = 80 cm in Kisumu), updated their cumulative watermelon model with the formula and labelled sector areas, and added the connecting sentence: 'This formula tells the mama mboga exactly how much watermelon any wedge contains so every customer is charged fairly by area.'

LESSONS.title: Lesson 5 — From Wedge to Segment: Deriving and Applying the Area of a Circular Segment
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle
LESSONS.aresKeywords: area of segment, circular segment, sector minus triangle, chord, segment calculation

slo.purpose: Learners derive the formula for the area of a circular segment by recognising it as the difference between a sector and a triangle, then apply this to determine the true area of the curved rind-bounded piece left when Mama Achieng's watermelon slice is cut straight across the chord.
slo.knowledge:
• A circular segment is the region between a chord and the arc it cuts off.
• The area of a segment = Area of sector − Area of triangle, i.e. A = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ.
• The triangle inside a sector formed by two radii and a chord has area = ½r²sin θ, where θ is the central angle in degrees.
slo.skills:
• Calculate the area of the isosceles triangle formed by two radii and a chord using A = ½r²sin θ.
• Derive and apply the segment area formula A = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ to solve real-life problems involving curved shapes.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that breaking a complex shape into familiar parts (sector and triangle) is a powerful mathematical problem-solving strategy.
• Demonstrate curiosity and persistence when moving from the known sector formula to the new segment formula.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use the area of part of a circle — specifically a segment — in real life, and how do we calculate it exactly?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–4 established that the area of a sector = (θ/360) × πr². This lesson advances the storyline by asking: what if Mama Achieng cuts straight across the watermelon, creating a flat edge rather than a pointed wedge? That curved rind-bounded piece is a segment — a new shape the learners cannot yet calculate. By discovering that a segment = sector − triangle, learners unlock the second part-of-a-circle formula and move closer to fully solving any fair-sharing or design problem involving circular shapes.
slo.safetyNotes: No sharp instruments required. If physical circular cut-outs are used, scissors should be handled with care and passed handle-first. No other specific hazards.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the fifth in the evidence-gathering sequence and marks a conceptual turning point in the sub-strand storyline. Having spent Lessons 1–4 mastering the sector area formula, learners now encounter a genuinely new shape: the circular segment — the region trapped between a chord and its arc. The lesson is anchored in the Wakulima Market phenomenon: when Mama Achieng decides to cut straight across a watermelon wedge (slicing off the pointed tip along a flat chord), she creates a curved, rind-bounded piece whose area her customers cannot estimate using any formula learned so far. This creates the need for a new tool.

The lesson is structured around a guided discovery: learners first predict whether the segment is larger or smaller than the triangle that fits inside the same sector, then observe a visual decomposition (sector = triangle + segment, therefore segment = sector − triangle). Through the Explain phase, learners derive the segment formula step by step — Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr², Area of triangle = ½r²sin θ, therefore Area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ — and apply it to two Wakulima Market problems. The ½r²sin θ triangle formula is introduced here for the first time, connecting directly to the Trigonometry sub-strand (2.3) already studied.

By the end of the lesson learners update their Driving Question Board with the segment formula and revise their cumulative circle-part model to include both sectors and segments, clearly annotating the relationship between the two. Teacher moves are designed for a 40-minute period with deliberate wait times, targeted cold-calling, and a structured pair–share to ensure every learner constructs — rather than merely copies — the new formula.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a large circle diagram on the board (or a printed hand-out) in which a chord has been drawn across a sector of radius 14 cm and central angle 60°. The sector is shaded; the triangle inside it is outlined in a different colour. Learners individually write answers to two questions in their exercise books: (1) 'Which is larger — the shaded sector or the triangle inside it? By how much, roughly?' and (2) 'If I remove the triangle from the sector, what shape is left, and how would you describe its boundary?' After 2 minutes of silent individual writing, learners share predictions with a seat partner for 1 minute.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the diagram and read aloud: 'Look carefully at this circle. A chord has been drawn inside a sector. In your books, answer these two questions — work alone and in silence for two minutes. I want YOUR thinking, not your neighbour's.' [Allow 2 minutes of silent thinking — do not circulate or give hints during this time.] After 2 minutes: 'Now turn to your partner and share what you wrote. You have one minute — go.' [After 1 minute, cold-call 3 pairs — choose one stronger and two mid-range learners.] Ask pair 1: 'What did you both agree the leftover shape looks like?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Ask pair 2: 'Did you think the triangle was bigger or smaller than the sector? What was your reasoning?' [Wait 12 seconds.] Ask pair 3: 'Can you describe the boundary of that leftover shape in your own words?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Do NOT confirm or correct yet. Say: 'Hold those ideas — we are about to find out who is right.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict–Observe–Explain (POE) launch: By asking learners to commit a written prediction before any instruction, this strategy activates prior knowledge of sectors and triangles, surfaces misconceptions about curved boundaries, and creates genuine cognitive need to observe the decomposition. The prediction becomes a personal stake in the upcoming evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written responses during the silent phase, noting (a) whether learners correctly identify the sector as larger than the triangle, and (b) whether they can describe the segment boundary as 'an arc and a straight line (chord)'. Learners who describe the leftover shape as 'another triangle' or 'a rectangle' signal a gap in understanding curved boundaries — flag these learners for targeted questioning in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive (or draw) a circle of radius 14 cm with a 60° sector clearly marked. They physically cut out (or shade-and-label on paper) three regions: the full sector, the isosceles triangle formed by the two radii and the chord, and the remaining curved piece (the segment). Working in groups of three, learners measure the chord length using a ruler, label each region, and record: 'Sector = Triangle + Segment, therefore Segment = Sector − Triangle.' They then calculate the sector area using the formula they already know — (60/360) × π × 14² — and record the numerical result. They also note the shape of the triangle (two equal sides of 14 cm, included angle 60°, making it equilateral) and estimate the triangle's area by counting squares on graph paper or by recalling the triangle area formula from Sub-Strand 2.4.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute cut-out circles (or direct learners to draw a 14 cm radius circle using compasses). Say: 'In your group of three, cut out — or shade on paper — the sector with angle 60°. Then draw the chord connecting the two ends of the arc. Now you have three regions. Label them: call the big curved slice SECTOR, call the pointy triangle TRIANGLE, and call the curved bit left between the chord and the arc SEGMENT.' [Circulate for 3 minutes, checking labelling. If a group is stuck: 'Show me where the chord is. Good. Everything on the arc side of that chord — what shape is that?'] After groups label correctly, say: 'Now write this relationship in your books: Sector = Triangle + Segment. Rearrange it — what does Segment equal?' [Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call one group who has not yet spoken today.] 'Correct — Segment = Sector minus Triangle. Now calculate the sector area using the formula we proved in Lesson 2. Write the substitution step, not just the answer.' [Allow 3 minutes. Circulate and check substitution is written as (60/360) × π × 14².] Say: 'Look at your triangle. Its two equal sides are both radii — 14 cm each — and the angle between them is 60°. What kind of triangle is that?' [Wait 10 seconds. Cold-call a learner who predicted incorrectly in the Predict phase.] 'Yes — equilateral. We will use that in the next phase to find its area exactly.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Decomposition and Reassembly (Breaking Complex into Known Parts): Learners physically or visually separate the segment from the sector, making the abstract relationship Segment = Sector − Triangle concrete and manipulable. This strategy mirrors the NGSS Science and Engineering Practice of 'Analysing and Interpreting Data' — learners extract a structural relationship from a physical object rather than receiving it as a rule.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks that every group has correctly written 'Segment = Sector − Triangle' before moving on. Key observable indicators: (1) The chord is drawn as a straight line connecting the two arc endpoints — not a curve. (2) The segment is identified as the region on the arc side of the chord, not the triangle side. (3) The sector area is calculated with a written substitution step showing (60/360) × π × 14². Groups that shade the wrong region (the major segment instead of the minor) should be redirected immediately with the question: 'Which piece is smaller — the one with the arc close to the chord, or the big curved piece? We are working with the smaller one.'

framework.learnerExperience: The class derives the triangle area formula ½r²sin θ together, guided by the teacher. Learners substitute values (r = 14, θ = 60°) to find the triangle area, then subtract from the sector area to find the segment area. They record the general formula: Area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ. Learners then individually solve two Wakulima Market problems: (A) Mama Achieng cuts a 90° sector from her 14 cm radius watermelon and then slices off the pointed tip along a chord — find the segment area; (B) A market stall designer in Kenyatta Market, Nairobi, wants to tile a curved decorative panel that is a segment of a circle with radius 20 cm and central angle 120° — find the area of the panel. Learners write full working, including formula statement, substitution, and answer with units.
framework.teacherMoves: Write on the board: 'We know: Area of triangle = ½ × base × height. For our isosceles triangle with two sides of length r and included angle θ, there is a trigonometry shortcut.' Ask: 'From Sub-Strand 2.3, if I know two sides and the included angle of a triangle, what formula gives me the area?' [Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call a learner from the Trigonometry unit.] If no response: 'The formula is ½ × a × b × sin C. Here, a = b = r and C = θ. So area of our triangle = ½ × r × r × sin θ = ½r²sin θ.' Write this step by step. Say: 'Now substitute r = 14, θ = 60° and calculate ½ × 14² × sin 60°. Use your calculator. Write the substitution first.' [Allow 90 seconds. Walk to three different tables to check calculator use and substitution.] Cold-call one learner for the numerical answer. Confirm: ½ × 196 × 0.8660 ≈ 84.87 cm². Then say: 'Now subtract your triangle area from your sector area to get the segment area. Do this in your books.' [Wait 2 minutes.] 'So our general formula is...' [write slowly, pointing to each term]: 'Area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ.' Say: 'Copy this formula with a box around it. It is the second major formula of this sub-strand.' Then: 'You have 6 minutes — solve both Wakulima Market and Kenyatta Market problems in your books. Show every step. Problem A: 90°, r = 14 cm. Problem B: 120°, r = 20 cm. Go.' [Circulate; after 6 minutes cold-call two different learners to present their working for A and B respectively at the board. For each presenter: 'Talk us through your substitution step by step.' Correct errors publicly and positively.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked Example → Generalise → Apply (Gradual Release): The teacher models one full numerical example with the class, then immediately releases learners to apply the generalised formula to two new contexts. Connecting ½r²sin θ to the already-known two-sides-and-included-angle triangle formula (Sub-Strand 2.3 Trigonometry) makes the new step a logical extension rather than an isolated rule, reinforcing cross-strand coherence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher looks for three specific things in written working: (1) The formula is stated before substitution — not just a numerical calculation. (2) sin 90° = 1 is correctly applied in Problem A (many learners mistakenly write sin 90° as 0.9 or omit it). (3) Units are written as cm². For Problem B, a common error is subtracting the triangle area before computing it — teacher watches for premature subtraction. Any learner who gets a negative segment area has subtracted in the wrong order and needs immediate one-to-one redirection.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. Each learner writes one sticky note (or contributes to a shared poster) responding to the prompt: 'What new tool did we add today for calculating a part of a circle, and when would Mama Achieng need it instead of the sector formula?' Learners post their notes under the column 'What We Now Know'. The class then reads three posted notes aloud and discusses whether the DQB driving question — about calculating the exact area of any wedge-shaped or segment-shaped piece — can now be more fully answered. A class scribe adds the segment formula to the 'Our Growing Formula Bank' section of the DQB.
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners to the DQB: 'We started this unit with Mama Achieng's watermelon at Wakulima Market. Our driving question asked about wedge-shaped AND segment-shaped pieces. Until today, we could only handle wedge shapes — sectors. What changed today?' [Wait 12 seconds. Take 3 raised hands — not cold-call here, as this is a public knowledge-building moment.] After responses: 'Write on your sticky note: one formula and one real-life situation where you would use a segment rather than a sector. You have 90 seconds — write now.' [After 90 seconds, direct learners to post notes.] Read three notes aloud — choose one strong, one partial, one that contains a misconception. For the misconception note (e.g. 'use segment whenever you have a circle'), say: 'This learner is asking a great implied question — when exactly do you have a segment? Let's clarify: a segment appears when...' [Prompt class.] After: 'Scribe, please add today's formula to the Formula Bank section.' [Dictate clearly: Area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public Knowledge Aggregation (Driving Question Board Update): The DQB functions as a living class document that maps growing understanding against the original phenomenon. Posting sticky notes externalises individual thinking and makes patterns of understanding — and gaps — visible to the whole class and teacher simultaneously. Revisiting the driving question at this stage reinforces that each lesson is a step in an ongoing investigation, not an isolated topic.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all posted sticky notes during or immediately after the DQB phase. Indicators of strong understanding: learner correctly identifies that a segment needs a chord (flat cut), whereas a sector needs two radii meeting at a point. Indicators of confusion: learner conflates segment and sector, or cannot state when each is used. These learners are identified for targeted follow-up in the next lesson's Predict phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their cumulative 'Circle Parts Model' — a diagram they have been building across Lessons 1–4 showing a circle divided into sectors with annotations of the sector formula. Today they add a new layer: they draw a chord across one sector, shade the resulting segment, and annotate it with the segment formula. They also add a 'decision tree' annotation beside their model: 'If the shape has two radii and an arc → use SECTOR formula. If the shape has one chord and an arc → use SEGMENT formula.' Learners write a one-sentence 'model update statement' beneath their diagram explaining what new understanding the segment formula adds to their ability to answer the driving question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your Circle Parts Model from your portfolio. You have been building this since Lesson 1. Today we add the segment.' Give explicit instructions: 'Step 1 — draw a chord across one of your existing sectors. Step 2 — shade the segment (the region between the chord and the arc). Step 3 — write the segment formula as an annotation with an arrow pointing to the shaded region. Step 4 — add the decision tree I am about to write on the board.' [Write on board: TWO RADII + ARC → SECTOR → A = (θ/360)πr². ONE CHORD + ARC → SEGMENT → A = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sin θ.] 'You have 4 minutes for steps 1–4. Begin.' [Circulate; after 4 minutes cold-call one learner: 'Read me your model update statement.' Then ask a second: 'In your model, point to the segment and tell me the two parts you subtract to find its area.' Wait 10 seconds each time.] Close with: 'Today Mama Achieng's customers can now ask about ANY curved piece of her watermelon — wedge or flat-cut slice — and we have the exact formula to answer them. Next lesson we will use both formulas together to solve a full fair-sharing design problem.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Progressive Diagram Annotation): The circle model serves as a running scientific model that is revised as understanding deepens — directly mirroring the NGSS practice of 'Developing and Using Models'. The decision tree annotation is a metacognitive tool that helps learners self-monitor which formula to select in novel problems, building flexible procedural knowledge rather than rote application.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks that (1) the chord is drawn as a straight line across an existing sector (not a new freehand curve), (2) the segment is shaded on the arc side of the chord (not the triangle side), (3) both the formula annotation and the decision tree are present and correctly written. The one-sentence model update statement is the richest formative indicator: a complete sentence such as 'The segment formula lets me find the area of any curved piece of a circle that is bounded by a chord and an arc, not just a wedge' shows full integration; a statement such as 'I learned the segment formula' shows surface engagement only.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Explain phase, did ALL learners correctly apply sin 90° = 1 in Problem A, or did a significant number treat it as a decimal approximation? If the latter, how will I address the exact trigonometric values (sin 30°, sin 60°, sin 90°) at the start of Lesson 6?
2. When learners updated the Driving Question Board, how many sticky notes demonstrated a clear distinction between a sector and a segment (two radii vs. one chord)? Were there learners who still conflated the two shapes, and how will I re-expose them to that boundary condition?
3. Did the connection to Sub-Strand 2.3 (½ab sin C) feel natural to learners, or did it seem like a new and unrelated formula? What does this tell me about the extent to which learners are building an integrated, cross-strand mathematical toolkit rather than isolated rules?
4. Was the 40-minute period sufficient for learners to complete both Wakulima Market problems with full written working, or did time pressure cause learners to skip the formula-statement step? If many skipped this step, what classroom norm do I need to reinforce?
5. Looking at the cumulative Circle Parts Models learners updated today, are the decision trees accurate and do they reflect genuine understanding of when to choose each formula? Which learners' models suggest they are ready for the combined-problem challenge planned for Lesson 6, and which learners need a consolidation activity before moving on?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed that when a chord is drawn across a sector of Mama Achieng's 14 cm radius watermelon, the sector is divided into two distinct regions — an isosceles triangle (formed by the two radii and the chord) and a curved segment (the region between the chord and the arc). They saw physically and numerically that Segment = Sector − Triangle, and verified this with the specific case of a 60° sector.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a circular segment is found by subtracting the area of the isosceles triangle from the area of the sector that contains it: Area of segment = (θ/360) × πr² − ½r²sin θ. The triangle's area is calculated using the two-sides-and-included-angle formula ½r²sin θ, which connects directly to the Trigonometry sub-strand. A segment is bounded by one chord and one arc; a sector is bounded by two radii and one arc — these require different formulas.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The phenomenon involves two types of curved pieces: the pointed wedge (sector) and the flat-cut curved rind-piece (segment). Now that learners have both the sector formula (Lessons 1–4) and the segment formula (Lesson 5), they can calculate the exact area of ANY piece Mama Achieng cuts from her watermelon — whether she cuts along two radii (a sector) or along a chord (a segment). This means a customer at Wakulima Market can now verify mathematically, not just visually, whether their flat-cut curved slice is a fair share.

LESSONS.title: Formalising the Sector Area Formula: From Watermelon Wedges to Irrigation Arcs
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle

slo.purpose: To formalise the sector area formula and apply it fluently to graduated real-life Kenyan contexts — from a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market to a school gate swing to a centre-pivot irrigation arc — so that learners can calculate the exact area of any sector and justify their reasoning to peers.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know: (a) the sector area formula A = (θ/360) × πr² for a central angle θ in degrees; (b) that sector area scales proportionally with both the angle θ and the square of the radius r; (c) how to identify radius and central angle from real-life sector-shaped objects in Kenya.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) derive and state the sector area formula from their group findings in prior lessons; (b) substitute values accurately into A = (θ/360) × πr² and compute area in cm², m², and hectares; (c) present and evaluate worked solutions in pairs and as a class; (d) update the Driving Question Board with the formalised formula and a new arising question.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate: (a) the power of a single formula to resolve the 'unfair watermelon slice' dispute at Wakulima Market; (b) the role of mathematics in fair-sharing and real-world design problems; (c) the value of collaboration and peer evaluation in consolidating mathematical understanding.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–5 learners gathered evidence — measuring cut-outs of sectors, observing angle-area relationships, and working in groups to hypothesise a formula. In Lesson 6 the teacher formalises that formula, anchors it to three graduated Kenyan contexts (watermelon slice, school gate arc, irrigation pivot), and learners practise applying it in pairs before updating the DQB. This lesson moves the class from evidence-gathering to explanation, directly answering the driving question's demand for an exact calculation method.
slo.safetyNotes: No significant hazards. If physical circular cut-outs or compasses are used for illustration, remind learners to handle compass points with care. Ensure adequate desk space when pairs spread out workbooks for peer evaluation.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 6 of 8 in the evidence-gathering sequence. The teacher opens by projecting the Wakulima Market watermelon phenomenon and asking pairs to recall their group formula hypotheses from Lesson 5. After a brief Predict phase, the teacher formalises A = (θ/360) × πr² through a whole-class derivation anchored to the phenomenon. Learners then work through three graduated Kenyan context examples — (1) a 120° watermelon slice of radius 15 cm, (2) a school gate of radius 1.2 m swinging through 75°, (3) a centre-pivot irrigation arc of radius 80 m through 270° — first as a guided worked example, then in pairs, then independently. Pairs present solutions on mini-whiteboards for class evaluation. The lesson closes with DQB updating: learners add the formalised formula and post one new question that has arisen. Teacher reflection data are gathered via an exit card. Connects directly to KICD SLO (a): determine the area of a sector of a circle in different situations, and SLO (c): apply the area of part of a circle in real-life situations.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their exercise books to their Lesson 5 group hypothesis for the sector area formula. Working individually for 2 minutes, each learner writes a prediction: 'Using my group's formula from last lesson, what area (in cm²) would a watermelon sector of radius 15 cm and angle 120° have?' They record their prediction and reasoning in one sentence. After individual thinking, pairs compare predictions and note whether they agree or differ, circling the part of their formula they are least confident about. Predictions remain visible on the desk throughout the lesson as a reference point.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Wakulima Market image on the board (or sketch a large circle with two radii drawn at 120°, labelled 'watermelon, r = 15 cm, θ = 120°'). Say verbatim: 'Last lesson your groups proposed a formula for sector area. Before I show you anything new, I want you to trust your own thinking. Individually — not with your partner yet — use your group's formula and predict the area of this 120° slice. Write your answer and one sentence explaining why.' Allow 2 minutes of silent individual work. Then say: 'Now turn to your partner. Compare your answers. If they differ, identify exactly which part of the formula caused the difference.' Allow 2 minutes of pair talk. Cold-call 3 pairs (choose one pair whose prediction is correct, one slightly off, one using a different but plausible approach). For each, ask: 'Walk us through your formula — where does each part come from?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each cold-call before accepting response. Record the three predictions on the board in a column headed 'Our Predictions' without evaluating them yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Predict-Before-Instruction (PBI) anchored to the phenomenon. By committing a specific numerical prediction to paper before instruction, learners activate their existing mental models from Lessons 1–5. Displaying competing predictions on the board creates productive cognitive dissonance — learners are motivated to find out which prediction the formalised formula will confirm, directly tying the formula derivation to a felt need.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has a written numerical prediction and a reasoning sentence before pair talk begins. Teacher circulates during individual work (2 min) and notes: (a) which learners use a proportional structure (θ/360 × something) — these have the key conceptual anchor; (b) which learners attempt an additive or unrelated approach — these need targeted support during the Explain phase. Teacher uses this scan to select the three pairs for cold-call to represent the range of thinking in the room.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher projects or draws a full circle of radius r and shades a sector of angle θ. Learners observe as the teacher builds the derivation step-by-step on the board, with learners completing a structured note-frame in their books simultaneously. The note-frame has five gaps: (1) Area of full circle = ___; (2) A full circle has a central angle of ___°; (3) A sector with angle θ is ___ of the full circle; (4) Therefore, area of sector = ___ × area of full circle; (5) Simplified formula: A = ___. After the derivation, learners observe three physical demonstrations of scale: teacher sketches a 30° sector, a 120° sector, and a 270° sector of the same radius on the board and asks learners to use the formula to rank them by area before computing — reconnecting to the watermelon vendor's problem of unequal-looking slices.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Let's build the formula together from first principles — the same logic your groups were using.' Draw a full circle, label radius r. Step 1 — write 'Full circle area = πr²' and ask: 'Why πr²? Shout it out.' (Accept responses, reinforce.) Step 2 — draw a sector, label θ. Ask: 'If the full circle is 360°, what FRACTION of the circle is this sector?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. Step 3 — write 'Sector area = (θ/360) × πr²' on the board in a box. Say: 'Write this formula in your note-frame and say it out loud to your partner twice.' (30 seconds.) Step 4 — return to the prediction column on the board. Say: 'Look at our three predictions from earlier. Using this formula, which prediction was correct? Put a tick next to the correct one in your own notes.' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners to explain the tick. Step 5 — sketch the three sectors (30°, 120°, 270°, same r) and say: 'Before you calculate anything, rank these three sectors by area — smallest to largest. Write your ranking.' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Then ask 2 learners to justify their ranking. Confirm: 'Area grows with angle — this is exactly why the mama mboga's customers with 30° slices were complaining!'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Structured Note-Frame Derivation with Prediction Revisit. The note-frame ensures learners are not passive — they construct the formula in writing at the same time as the teacher. The immediate return to the prediction column closes the predict–observe loop: learners experience the formula as the resolution of their earlier uncertainty rather than as an imposed rule. The three-sector ranking task uses relational reasoning (proportionality) before computation, building conceptual understanding ahead of procedural practice.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: All five gaps in the note-frame are completed correctly. Teacher does a 30-second visual scan of note-frames before moving on — specifically checking gap (3) ('θ/360 of the full circle') as this is the proportionality concept most likely to be incomplete. If more than 4 learners have gap (3) blank or incorrect, teacher pauses and re-teaches the fraction-of-a-full-turn idea using: 'If Amina gets 1 slice out of 3 equal slices, what fraction does she get? If her slice angle is 120° out of 360°, what fraction is that?' before proceeding.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work through three graduated examples in Kenyan contexts, progressing from guided (teacher-led) to paired to individual. EXAMPLE 1 (Guided, whole class — 8 min): Watermelon slice. A circular watermelon at Wakulima Market has radius 15 cm. A vendor cuts a sector of angle 120°. Calculate the exact area of the slice in cm², giving the answer in terms of π and as a decimal (use π = 3.142). Learners follow the teacher's worked solution on the board, completing each calculation step in their books simultaneously. EXAMPLE 2 (Paired — 10 min): School gate. A metal school gate rotates about a hinge post. The gate arm is 1.2 m long. When fully opened, it sweeps through an angle of 75°. Calculate the area of ground swept by the gate in m², correct to 3 significant figures. Pairs work side-by-side; one partner writes the formula substitution, the other writes the numerical evaluation, then they swap roles to check. One pair is selected to present on a mini-whiteboard. Class evaluates using two criteria on the board: (i) correct formula substitution, (ii) correct arithmetic. EXAMPLE 3 (Independent — 12 min): Centre-pivot irrigation. A centre-pivot irrigation system near Naivasha has an arm of radius 80 m. The system currently operates over a sector of 270°. Calculate: (a) the area irrigated in m²; (b) the area in hectares (1 hectare = 10,000 m²). Learners work independently and silently. After 10 minutes, pairs peer-mark using the answer written on the board. Learners who finish early are challenged: 'The farmer wants to expand the system to cover the full circle. How many additional m² would be irrigated?'
framework.teacherMoves: EXAMPLE 1: Write the problem on the board. Say: 'This is our mama mboga's exact slice — 120°, radius 15 cm. We are going to solve it together step by step. I write, you write.' Narrate each step aloud: 'Step 1 — identify what we know: θ = 120°, r = 15 cm. Step 2 — write the formula: A = (θ/360) × πr². Step 3 — substitute: A = (120/360) × π × 15². Step 4 — simplify the fraction: 120/360 = 1/3. Step 5 — work out 15² = 225. Step 6 — A = (1/3) × π × 225 = 75π cm². Step 7 — decimal: 75 × 3.142 = 235.65 cm².' Pause after each step for learners to write. After Step 4 ask: 'Why did 120/360 simplify to 1/3? What does that tell us about this slice?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. After completing: 'So the customer's slice is exactly 235.65 cm². If the vendor claims all slices are equal but another customer's slice is 180° — how large is that slice? Do the maths in your head.' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. EXAMPLE 2: Write the gate problem. Say: 'With your partner — one of you writes the formula and substitution, the other evaluates the arithmetic. Then swap and check each other. You have 8 minutes.' Circulate and target pairs where substitution errors appear (common error: using diameter instead of radius). Ask targeted prompt: 'The formula uses r — what is r here? Is 1.2 m the radius or the diameter?' After 8 minutes, invite one pair to present on a mini-whiteboard. Say to the class: 'Evaluate this solution on two criteria — correct formula setup, and correct arithmetic. Give a thumbs up for each criterion you agree with.' Address any arithmetic errors whole-class. EXAMPLE 3: Say: 'This one is yours — independent, silent. Read carefully — there are two parts, and part (b) requires a unit conversion.' Circulate silently. After 10 minutes say: 'Exchange books with your partner. I'll write the answers on the board — mark part (a) and part (b) separately.' Write: 'A = (270/360) × π × 80² = (3/4) × 3.142 × 6400 = 15,079.6 m²; in hectares = 1.508 ha.' After peer marking ask: 'Raise your hand if you got both parts correct.' Then: 'Raise your hand if you got part (a) correct but made a unit conversion error in part (b).' Address unit conversion error directly: 'Dividing by 10,000 — is the answer going to be bigger or smaller than your m² answer? Why?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Gradual Release of Responsibility (I Do → We Do → You Do) within a Kenyan Context Progression. Each example escalates in two dimensions simultaneously: (1) computational demand (integer angle that simplifies → decimal angle → reflex angle with unit conversion), and (2) physical scale (kitchen-table watermelon → school compound gate → commercial farm). This progression re-anchors each calculation to the driving question's real-life scope, showing learners that one formula handles wedge-shaped problems from centimetres to metres to hectares. Pair presentation and class evaluation using explicit criteria (formula setup, arithmetic) make peer assessment a sensemaking activity rather than a social exercise.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) During Example 1, all learners have seven written steps in their books — teacher scans before moving to Example 2. (2) During Example 2 circulation, teacher specifically checks whether the pair with the most errors in Lessons 1–5 (identified from prior lesson records) can write A = (75/360) × π × 1.2² correctly. (3) After Example 3 peer marking, teacher tallies show-of-hands data: if more than 6 learners got part (a) wrong, teacher re-does the 270° substitution (common error: subtracting 270 from 360 first). If more than 8 learners got the unit conversion wrong, teacher spends 2 additional minutes on the hectare conversion with a second Naivasha farm example before closing.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front. Individually, each learner writes two sticky-note responses: (1) a FORMULA CARD — they write the sector area formula A = (θ/360) × πr² in their own words and add a one-line explanation of what each symbol means in the context of the watermelon phenomenon (e.g., 'θ is the angle the vendor cuts, r is how far the rind is from the centre'); (2) a NEW QUESTION CARD — they write one new question that arose during today's lesson that the formula alone does not yet answer (e.g., 'What if the piece of watermelon is not a full wedge but has the middle scooped out — how would we find that area?', or 'Can we use this formula if the angle is given in radians instead of degrees?'). Pairs read each other's new question cards and star the one they find most interesting. The teacher collects all formula cards for the DQB's 'What We Now Know' column and posts a selection of starred new question cards in the 'What We Still Wonder' column, reading two aloud to the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'For the last four minutes, I want two sticky notes from each of you — no sharing yet, individual thinking only. First sticky note: write the sector area formula and explain in your own words what θ and r mean for our watermelon problem. Second sticky note: write one new question that today's formula has NOT yet answered for you.' WAIT TIME: 4 minutes silent individual work. Then say: 'Read your partner's new question card. Put a star on the one that makes YOU most curious — it can be yours or theirs.' Allow 1 minute. Collect formula cards and post to DQB 'What We Now Know' column. Scan new question cards rapidly and select 2–3 that point toward Lesson 7 content (area of a segment — 'what if the straight edge is a chord, not two radii?'). Read these aloud and say: 'These questions are exactly where we are going in Lesson 7. Keep them — they are your intellectual compass.' Post selected new question cards to DQB 'What We Still Wonder' column.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: DQB Incremental Update with Metacognitive Framing. The DQB is a public, cumulative record of the class's growing understanding of the driving question. By requiring learners to translate the formula into their own language connected to the phenomenon (Formula Card), the teacher checks for conceptual ownership rather than rote memorisation. The New Question Card makes visible the productive confusion that genuine learning generates, and teacher selection of cards pointing toward Lesson 7 content models scientific inquiry — new knowledge raises new questions — while maintaining narrative continuity in the storyline.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Formula cards that use the watermelon context in their explanation (not just abstract symbols) indicate conceptual connection to the phenomenon — teacher counts these as a ratio. Target: ≥ 70% of cards include a phenomenon-linked explanation. (2) New question cards that reference 'segment', 'chord', 'arc length', or 'radian' indicate learners whose thinking is running ahead of the sequence — teacher notes these learners for differentiation in Lesson 7. (3) New question cards that re-ask a question already answered (e.g., 'Why does angle affect area?') indicate learners who have not yet consolidated today's key idea — teacher notes these learners for a brief one-to-one check-in at the start of Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the cumulative Sector-Segment Model diagram they have been building since Lesson 1 (a circle with labelled parts, annotated with their growing understanding). Today's task: each learner adds three things to their model — (1) the formalised sector area formula in a labelled box connected by an arrow to the shaded sector region of their diagram; (2) a worked mini-example directly on the diagram using the watermelon context (θ = 120°, r = 15 cm → A = 75π ≈ 235.65 cm²) annotated with each substitution step; (3) a 'Scaling Note' — they shade three different-sized sectors on a small circle sketch and write: 'Doubling the angle doubles the area. Doubling the radius quadruples the area.' This note captures the proportionality insight that explains why the vendor's customers see such dramatically different wedge sizes. Learners who complete all three additions early begin sketching what a segment (sector minus triangle) might look like on their model, in preparation for Lesson 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative model diagram. Today you are adding the formula, a worked example, and a scaling note — these three additions together answer the core question: WHY does changing only the angle change the area so dramatically? Add them now. You have 12 minutes.' Circulate and prompt: (a) To learners who have written the formula without connecting it to the diagram: 'Draw an arrow from your formula box to the shaded sector. Label the arrow with what the formula calculates.' (b) To learners who have the worked example but no scaling note: 'Now I want you to think about the r² part. If the vendor doubled the radius of her watermelon from 15 cm to 30 cm, keeping the angle at 120°, would the area double? Triple? Quadruple? Write the scaling note.' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds for each prompted learner to think before responding. After 12 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to share their scaling note. Ask the class: 'Does everyone agree that doubling r quadruples the area? Convince me with numbers — someone use the formula for r=15 and r=30 right now.' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner to verify. Spend final 2 minutes on exit card (see Formative Assessment).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Strategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Explicit Scaling Analysis. The cumulative model functions as a personal knowledge-building artefact across all 8 lessons — each addition is not a new diagram but an annotation layer on the same evolving representation. The 'Scaling Note' is the key sensemaking move of this lesson: it asks learners to articulate the r² relationship in plain language, which directly explains the phenomenon (why a small change in angle or radius makes wedges look dramatically different). This connects back to the driving question — 'Why does changing only the angle change the area so dramatically?' — and ensures the formula is understood as a model of a real relationship, not a calculation recipe.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators (Exit Card — 3 minutes at end of Model Building): Teacher writes two questions on the board. Learners answer on a half-sheet of paper to hand in. Q1 (procedural): 'A sector has radius 6 cm and angle 150°. Calculate its area correct to 1 decimal place. (Use π = 3.142.)' [Expected: A = (150/360) × 3.142 × 36 = 47.1 cm²] Q2 (conceptual — connects to phenomenon): 'A vendor at Wakulima Market cuts two slices from the same watermelon. Slice A has angle 60°, Slice B has angle 120°. Without calculating, how many times larger is Slice B than Slice A? Explain your reasoning in one sentence.' [Expected: Slice B is exactly 2 times larger because area is proportional to angle — doubling the angle doubles the area.] Teacher sorts exit cards into three piles after class: (Pile 1) Both correct — ready for Lesson 7 segment work; (Pile 2) Q1 correct, Q2 incorrect — procedural fluency but proportionality concept not yet secure; (Pile 3) Q1 incorrect — formula application errors to address at start of Lesson 7 with a 3-minute re-teach.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your lesson journal:
1. PHENOMENON CONNECTION: In how many of the five phases did you explicitly name the Wakulima Market watermelon vendor? If fewer than four, identify which phase lost the phenomenological thread and plan how to restore it in Lesson 7.
2. FORMULA OWNERSHIP: When you cold-called learners to explain the formula after the derivation, what language did they use? Did learners say 'θ over 360 is the fraction of the circle' (conceptual) or simply 'you plug in the numbers' (procedural)? How will you deepen conceptual language in Lesson 7's segment derivation?
3. GRADUATED EXAMPLES: Which of the three examples (watermelon, gate, irrigation pivot) caused the most difficulty? If the unit conversion in Example 3 (m² to hectares) caused widespread errors, consider whether Lesson 7 should open with a brief unit-conversion warm-up before introducing the segment formula.
4. DQB QUALITY: Count the proportion of New Question Cards that referenced 'segment', 'chord', or 'arc length' — this is your leading indicator of readiness for Lesson 7. If fewer than 30% of learners generated such questions, plan a brief 'Look at this shape' hook at the start of Lesson 7 to explicitly create the need for segment area.
5. EXIT CARD DATA: Use the three exit-card piles to inform Lesson 7 groupings. Consider pairing a Pile 1 learner with a Pile 2 learner during Lesson 7's segment derivation activity, and plan a 3-minute whole-class re-entry activity for Pile 3 learners before the main lesson begins.
6. PACING: This lesson targets 80 minutes. If the Explain phase (Examples 1–3) ran beyond 35 minutes, identify which example consumed excess time and whether learners needed more scaffolding on the 270° reflex angle or the r² scaling idea — both are critical for Lesson 7's segment work.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed a teacher-led step-by-step derivation of the sector area formula A = (θ/360) × πr² from first principles, built on the Wakulima Market watermelon phenomenon. They also observed three real-life Kenyan sector contexts: a 120° watermelon slice (r = 15 cm), a school gate sweep (r = 1.2 m, θ = 75°), and a Naivasha centre-pivot irrigation arc (r = 80 m, θ = 270°). Learners observed peer pair presentations on mini-whiteboards and whole-class evaluation of solution accuracy.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners learned that the area of any sector is a proportional fraction of the full circle's area, expressed as A = (θ/360) × πr². They learned that sector area scales linearly with angle θ (doubling the angle doubles the area) and quadratically with radius r (doubling the radius quadruples the area). They applied this formula to calculate areas in cm², m², and hectares across three graduated Kenyan contexts, and updated the class Driving Question Board with the formalised formula and new arising questions pointing toward segment area in Lesson 7.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained in their cumulative model diagrams and DQB Formula Cards why changing only the angle of a cut at Wakulima Market changes the area of the watermelon wedge so dramatically: because sector area is directly proportional to the central angle (A ∝ θ), a vendor who cuts at 120° instead of 60° produces a slice exactly twice as large — resolving the customers' complaint with mathematical precision. Learners also explained the r² relationship in a written Scaling Note, and exit card responses documented both procedural fluency (correct substitution) and conceptual understanding (proportionality reasoning without calculation).
