LESSONS.title: Investigating Segment Area: From Sector to Slice — Unlocking the Curved Piece
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle

slo.purpose: Learners will determine the area of a segment of a circle by subtracting the area of a triangle from the area of a sector, and apply this to solve fair-sharing problems rooted in the Wakulima Market watermelon phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (a) a segment is the region between a chord and the arc it subtends; (b) the area of a segment = area of sector − area of triangle (Area = ½r²θ − ½r²sinθ, where θ is in radians, OR Area = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ, where θ is in degrees); (c) the triangle formed by two radii and a chord has area ½r²sinθ.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) identify and distinguish a segment from a sector in a diagram; (b) calculate the area of the triangle formed by two radii and a chord using the formula ½r²sinθ; (c) compute the area of a segment by subtracting the triangle area from the sector area; (d) apply segment area to real-life contexts such as watermelon slices and design problems.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate how precise mathematical reasoning — rather than visual estimation — is the only reliable tool for ensuring fairness in real-life sharing situations. Learners display Unity by working collaboratively on cut-out investigations, and Peace by tolerating different approaches to solving segment problems.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–6, learners mastered sector area and explored how changing the angle of a cut changes the wedge size. But the mama mboga at Wakulima Market sometimes cuts watermelon so that the rind (the curved edge) falls away, leaving the customer with only the red flesh — a shape bounded by a chord and an arc: a segment. This lesson investigates: how much red flesh (segment area) does a customer actually receive? This is the key missing piece in the evidence sequence — learners now have all the tools needed to solve the full fair-sharing puzzle.
slo.safetyNotes: If physical cutting tools (scissors, rulers) are used for paper cut-outs, learners should handle them carefully and place them flat on the desk when not in use. No sharp knives or actual watermelons are needed; paper or card cut-outs are sufficient.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 7 is the penultimate evidence-gathering lesson in the 8-lesson sequence on Area of Part of a Circle (Sub-Strand 2.5). Learners have previously established the sector area formula and explored how angle size drives sector area. In this lesson, they investigate the area of a circular segment — the region between a chord and its arc — using a cut-out decomposition activity: separating a sector into a triangle and a segment, measuring, calculating, and reconciling results. The anchoring phenomenon (the mama mboga at Wakulima Market cutting watermelon) is deepened: when the rind is removed, what remains is a segment, and fair pricing demands its exact area. By the end of the lesson, learners can compute segment area using Area(segment) = Area(sector) − Area(triangle) = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ, and they update both their Driving Question Board and their cumulative circle-area model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a large diagram on the board: a circle of radius 14 cm with a chord drawn across it, shading only the smaller region between the chord and the arc (a minor segment). The teacher reminds learners of the mama mboga scenario: 'She cuts a watermelon and the rind falls away. The customer receives only the red flesh — this shaded region.' Learners individually write a prediction in their exercise books: (a) Is the shaded segment larger or smaller than the sector with the same angle? (b) Estimate the area of the segment if the sector angle is 60° and r = 14 cm. They share predictions with a shoulder partner (Think-Pair-Share, 2 minutes). Three pairs are cold-called to share their estimates.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the diagram using a poster or drawn clearly on the board. Say: 'Look carefully at the shaded region. This is the piece of watermelon the customer receives after the rind is cut away. In your books, write: is this region bigger or smaller than the full sector wedge? Then estimate its area — your best mathematical guess — if r = 14 cm and the sector angle is 60°. You have 3 minutes working alone.' [WAIT 3 minutes.] 'Now share with your shoulder partner. Do you agree?' [WAIT 1 minute.] Cold-call exactly 3 pairs using the register: 'Pair 4 — Akinyi and Otieno — what did you predict and why?' After each response, probe: 'What formula or reasoning did you use to arrive at that estimate?' [WAIT 10 seconds after each probe before accepting responses.] Record the range of estimates on the board without confirming or denying correctness: 'We have predictions from ____ cm² to ____ cm². Let us find out who is closest and why.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with anchored estimation. This activates learners' prior knowledge of sector area (Lessons 4–6) and surfaces the key misconception that a segment is simply a smaller sector. By estimating before calculating, learners create cognitive dissonance that motivates the observation phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learners write a numerical estimate (not just 'smaller'). Listen for whether learners attempt to use the sector formula — this reveals whether sector area from Lessons 4–6 has been consolidated. Flag any learner who writes 'area = arc length × r' — this confuses arc and area and needs targeted correction in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Activity 1 — Cut-Out Decomposition (30 min, groups of 4): Each group receives a pre-drawn circle of radius 14 cm on card, with a sector of 60° clearly marked and a chord connecting the two radii endpoints. Learners label the parts: sector OAB, triangle OAB, and segment AB (the region between chord AB and arc AB). Step 1: Learners cut out the full sector. Step 2: They fold/cut along the chord to separate the triangle from the segment. Step 3: They calculate the sector area using (θ/360)πr² = (60/360) × π × 14² ≈ 102.6 cm². Step 4: They calculate the area of triangle OAB using ½r²sinθ = ½ × 14² × sin60° ≈ 84.9 cm². Step 5: They find segment area = 102.6 − 84.9 = 17.7 cm². Step 6: They physically place the triangle cut-out on the segment to verify that the triangle is larger. Activity 2 — Data Table (10 min): Each group completes a table for three different angles (60°, 90°, 120°) at r = 14 cm, recording: Sector Area, Triangle Area, Segment Area. Groups record results on a shared class table drawn on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials (pre-drawn card circles, scissors, rulers, calculators) and say: 'Today you will physically decompose a sector into two parts: a triangle and a segment. Your job is to find the area of just the curved piece — the red flesh of the watermelon, after the rind is gone.' Walk group to group every 4 minutes. At each group, ask: 'Point to the segment. Now point to the triangle. Which is bigger?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] If a group is stuck on the triangle area, prompt: 'We calculated the area of a triangle given two sides and an included angle in Sub-Strand 2.4. What was that formula?' [WAIT 15 seconds — do NOT supply the answer immediately.] When groups finish Step 5, ask: 'Does your segment area match your Phase 1 prediction? Why or why not?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] For the class data table, cold-call one representative from 4 different groups to fill in one row each. Say: 'Amina from Group 3, please write your 90° results on the board.' After all rows are filled, ask the class: 'What pattern do you notice as the angle increases? Does the segment always grow at the same rate as the sector?' [WAIT 15 seconds before cold-calling 2 learners.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete decomposition (cut-and-separate). Making the abstract formula tactile — physically separating the triangle from the segment — gives learners a concrete referent for the operation 'sector minus triangle.' The shared class data table introduces co-construction of evidence, a key NGSS science and engineering practice (Analysing and Interpreting Data). Learners see that the segment grows nonlinearly with angle because sinθ is not linear.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every group can correctly label the segment vs. the sector vs. the triangle on their cut-out (check by circulating). (b) Every learner records a numeric segment area for at least one angle in the data table. (c) Listen for the phrase 'sector minus triangle' — if groups say 'sector minus arc,' intervene immediately: 'An arc is a length, not an area. What shape are you subtracting?' Red flag: groups who subtract arc length from sector area. These learners need the Phase 3 explicit instruction most urgently — note their names.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to whole class. The teacher derives the segment area formula explicitly on the board, connecting each step to the cut-out. Learners copy into their books and then solve two worked examples independently before a peer-check. Worked Example 1 (Wakulima context): A watermelon of radius 21 cm is cut with a chord so that the sector angle is 90°. Calculate the area of the segment (the red flesh). Answer: Sector = (90/360) × π × 21² = 346.4 cm²; Triangle = ½ × 21² × sin90° = ½ × 441 × 1 = 220.5 cm²; Segment = 346.4 − 220.5 = 125.9 cm². Worked Example 2 (Design context): A circular window of radius 10 cm has a decorative segment with a 120° arc. Find the segment area. Answer: Sector = (120/360) × π × 100 = 104.7 cm²; Triangle = ½ × 100 × sin120° = 50 × 0.866 = 43.3 cm²; Segment = 104.7 − 43.3 = 61.4 cm². Learners then solve a third problem independently: a chapati of radius 12 cm is cut with a chord at 80°. Find the segment area. After 5 minutes, they swap books with a partner for peer-marking using the board solution.
framework.teacherMoves: Begin by connecting to the cut-out: 'We physically separated the sector into a triangle and a segment. The formula simply does that subtraction mathematically.' Write on the board step by step: 'Area of segment = Area of sector − Area of triangle.' Then: 'Area of sector = (θ/360) × π × r².' Then: 'Area of triangle OAB = ½ × r × r × sinθ = ½r²sinθ.' Then: 'Therefore: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ.' Box this formula. Say: 'This is the core formula for today. Write it, box it, and label every variable.' [WAIT 1 minute for all learners to write.] Work through Example 1 aloud, pausing at each substitution: 'What is θ here? What is r? What do I substitute into the sector formula first?' [WAIT 10 seconds after each question before cold-calling — cold-call 3 different learners across Example 1.] For Example 2, do the sector step only, then say: 'You complete the triangle step and the subtraction — 2 minutes, alone.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Cold-call 2 learners to give the triangle area and the final answer. For the independent chapati problem, say: 'Work entirely alone. Show every step. You have 5 minutes.' [WAIT 5 minutes strictly.] Then: 'Swap books. Mark your partner's work as I reveal the solution. Write one thing they did well and one thing to improve.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Explicit formula derivation anchored to the physical model (NGSS: Developing and Using Models). By connecting the algebraic formula to the physical cut-out, the teacher bridges concrete and abstract representations. Peer-marking builds metacognitive awareness and communication skills (KICD Core Competency: Communication and Collaboration). The Kenyan food contexts (watermelon, chapati) maintain the phenomenon thread throughout.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every learner's book contains the boxed formula with all variables labelled. (b) During the independent chapati problem, circulate and check that learners are using ½r²sinθ for the triangle (not ½ × base × height, which requires additional steps). (c) During peer-marking, listen for disagreements — these reveal common errors (e.g., forgetting to convert degrees to the correct trig input, or subtracting sector from triangle instead of the reverse). Cold-call one pair where the marker identified an error and ask: 'What mistake did you spot and how should it be corrected?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (DQB) displayed at the front. The DQB has been building since Lesson 1, tracking what learners know, what they wonder, and what evidence they have gathered. In pairs, learners write on sticky notes or designated DQB cards: (a) ONE new thing they can now explain about the watermelon phenomenon that they could not explain before this lesson; (b) ONE remaining question they still have about the fair-sharing problem. Pairs post their cards under the appropriate DQB columns ('Now I Can Explain…' and 'I Still Wonder…'). The teacher reads 3–4 cards aloud and the class votes on which remaining questions are most important to resolve in Lesson 8 (the final lesson).
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the DQB and say: 'Look at our board. At the start of this unit, we asked: how can we calculate the exact area of any wedge or segment of a circle, like the mama mboga's watermelon slices, so every customer gets a fair share? Today we unlocked the segment. Write on your card: one thing you can now explain about the phenomenon that you could not explain before.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] 'Now write your remaining question — what do you still need to know to fully solve the fair-sharing problem?' [WAIT 1 minute.] Ask pairs to post cards. Read 3–4 aloud, then say: 'Raise your hand if your remaining question is about applying both sector AND segment area together to solve a real problem.' Acknowledge hands: 'That is exactly what Lesson 8 will address. We are almost at the full answer to our driving question.' Highlight any DQB card that mentions comparing a segment and a sector from the same circle — this is the conceptual bridge to Lesson 8.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Update (metacognitive reflection and collective knowledge tracking). This strategy, used consistently across the 8-lesson sequence, makes learning visible and helps learners see their own progress along the storyline. Voting on remaining questions gives learners agency and primes them for Lesson 8. It also surfaces any persistent misconceptions (e.g., confusing segment and sector) that the teacher must address before the final lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every pair posts at least one 'Now I Can Explain' card that references segment area specifically (not just 'area of a circle'). (b) Teacher reads 'I Still Wonder' cards to check for productive questions (e.g., 'What if the angle is more than 180°?' or 'How do I find segment area without a calculator for sinθ?') vs. unproductive confusion (e.g., 'I don't understand anything about segments'). Learners with unproductive confusion cards are identified for targeted support before Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their cumulative circle-area model booklet (a folded A3 sheet that has been updated in each lesson). In Lessons 1–6, they drew and annotated: a full circle (area = πr²), a sector (area = (θ/360)πr²), and the relationship between angle and sector area. Today they add: a clearly labelled diagram of a circle showing a chord, a segment (shaded), the triangle OAB (unshaded), and the sector OAB (the sum). They write the segment area formula beside the diagram and annotate each component: 'This part is the sector,' 'This part is the triangle I subtract,' 'This shaded part is the segment — the red flesh.' They also add a second diagram: the Wakulima Market watermelon slice, labelled with r = 21 cm and θ = 90°, with the calculated segment area (125.9 cm²) written on the shaded region. Finally, learners write one sentence connecting today's model to the driving question: 'Now I can calculate the exact area of the red flesh in any watermelon segment, so I can check whether two pieces are truly equal even if one looks bigger.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model booklets to the next blank page. We are going to add the segment to our growing model of circle areas. First, draw a circle, mark the centre O, draw two radii OA and OB at 90°, then draw chord AB. Shade only the segment — the region between AB and the arc. Label: sector OAB, triangle OAB, segment AB.' [WAIT 3 minutes for drawing.] Circulate and check: 'Show me which part you are shading. Is that the segment or the sector?' [WAIT 10 seconds per group.] 'Now write the formula beside your diagram — box it.' [WAIT 1 minute.] 'Add the Wakulima watermelon diagram with r = 21 cm, θ = 90°, and the segment area we calculated: 125.9 cm².' [WAIT 2 minutes.] 'Finally, write one sentence: how does today's model help you answer the driving question?' Cold-call 2 learners to read their sentence aloud. Affirm and connect: 'Excellent. In Lesson 8 — our final evidence lesson — you will use BOTH the sector formula and the segment formula together to solve the complete fair-sharing problem for the mama mboga. Your model is almost complete.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision (NGSS: Developing and Using Models). The model booklet is the physical artefact of the entire 8-lesson storyline. Each revision makes the growing understanding visible and honours prior work. Writing a connecting sentence to the driving question is a disciplinary literacy move that consolidates conceptual understanding and prepares learners for the summative application in Lesson 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) Every learner's model diagram correctly distinguishes the segment (shaded) from the triangle (unshaded) and from the full sector. (b) The formula is written correctly and boxed. (c) The connecting sentence explicitly references the driving question ('fair share,' 'exact area,' 'watermelon,' or equivalent). Collect 5 model booklets (selected randomly) to review overnight and provide written feedback before Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Could all learners correctly identify the segment (not the sector) in the cut-out activity? If not, which groups confused the two, and how will you address this at the start of Lesson 8? (2) Did learners fluently apply the triangle area formula ½r²sinθ from Sub-Strand 2.4, or did the prerequisite knowledge create a bottleneck? If many learners struggled here, plan a 5-minute review of ½r²sinθ at the start of Lesson 8 before introducing combined applications. (3) Were the DQB 'I Still Wonder' cards mathematically productive? Do learners' remaining questions point toward the combined sector-and-segment application that Lesson 8 requires, or are there fundamental gaps that need to be closed first? (4) Review the 5 model booklets collected: are the diagrams correctly labelled and the formulas correctly written? Use findings to adjust the first 10 minutes of Lesson 8. (5) Did the Kenyan food contexts (watermelon at Wakulima Market, chapati) keep learners engaged and grounded in the phenomenon, or did the mathematical complexity cause some learners to lose the contextual thread? Plan to re-anchor the phenomenon explicitly at the opening of Lesson 8.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners cut out a sector of radius 14 cm and 60°, separated it into a triangle (OAB) and a segment, and calculated each area. They also completed a class data table for angles 60°, 90°, and 120°, recording sector area, triangle area, and segment area for each.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area of a segment = area of sector − area of triangle = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. The triangle formed by two radii and a chord has area ½r²sinθ. A segment is always smaller than its corresponding sector because the triangle area is always positive.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: For the mama mboga's watermelon at Wakulima Market: when the rind is removed, the customer receives a segment — the red flesh between the chord (cut face) and the curved rind arc. Using the segment formula, the exact area of red flesh in a 90° slice of radius 21 cm is 125.9 cm². This means we can now price each piece fairly by area, not by visual estimate.

LESSONS.title: Segment Area, Final Explanation & Fair-Share Verdict — Completing the Watermelon Puzzle
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle

slo.purpose: To determine the area of a segment of a circle and apply the area of part of a circle to real-life fair-sharing and design problems, culminating in a full explanation of the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that the area of a circular segment equals the area of the corresponding sector minus the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord; expressed as: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) identify and isolate the triangle inside a sector using a chord; (b) calculate the area of a triangle using ½r²sinθ; (c) subtract triangle area from sector area to find segment area; (d) apply both sector and segment formulae to solve fair-sharing and design problems; (e) construct and compare cumulative circle-area models from Lesson 1 through Lesson 8.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate how precise mathematical calculation — rather than visual guessing — guarantees fairness in real-life sharing situations, and will demonstrate confidence in presenting a complete, evidence-based explanation to peers.
slo.keyInquiry: Where do we use area of part of a circle in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In this final lesson learners return to their sector cut-outs from earlier lessons. By cutting out the triangle (formed by the two radii and the chord) from each sector, they isolate the segment and derive its area formula. They then use both sector and segment formulae to adjudicate the Wakulima Market watermelon dispute — calculating exactly how much watermelon (in cm²) each customer received — and revise their cumulative model one last time to produce a complete, evidence-based answer to the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors and cutting tools are to be handled with care; learners must cut away from their bodies and keep blades flat on the desk when not in use. Scrap paper pieces must be collected and disposed of responsibly to keep the classroom environment clean.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the capstone lesson for Sub-Strand 2.5. Learners begin with a Predict phase in which they estimate how much area is 'lost' when the triangular portion is removed from a sector to leave only the curved segment. In the Observe phase they physically cut the triangle from their sector cut-outs, measure dimensions, and record data. In the Explain phase they derive Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ, apply it to the Wakulima Market watermelon scenario (given realistic values: r = 18 cm, θ values of 40°, 65°, 90°, and 120°), and produce a fair-share verdict supported by calculations. The DQB phase marks all remaining questions as answered and surfaces the complete causal story. The Model Building phase invites learners to compare their Lesson 1 naïve drawing to their final annotated model, articulating every conceptual addition made across the unit. The lesson closes with a whole-class Final Explanation Gallery Walk and structured teacher-led consolidation.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group retrieves their sector cut-outs from previous lessons (r = 18 cm, various θ values). The teacher displays a large projected image of a watermelon sector with a straight chord drawn across it — separating the triangular piece (two radii + chord) from the curved segment (the rind-bounded sliver). Learners record individual written predictions in their science notebooks responding to two prompts: (1) 'Estimate: what fraction of the sector's area do you think the segment (the curved sliver beyond the chord) represents?' and (2) 'Will a wide-angle segment (θ = 120°) always have a larger area than a narrow-angle segment (θ = 40°) of the same radius? Explain your reasoning.' Groups share predictions via a quick show-of-hands poll on the fraction estimate, and the teacher records the spread of estimates on the board without confirming or correcting.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher opens by pointing to the projected watermelon image and saying: 'Last lesson we found the area of the full wedge — the sector. But look at this piece [points to the curved sliver beyond the chord]. A customer at Wakulima Market was sold ONLY this curved piece — no triangle. She says she was cheated. Was she? We need exact numbers.' Pause 10 seconds. Teacher writes both prediction prompts on the board and gives learners 3 minutes of silent individual thinking time. Teacher circulates, reading notebooks — do NOT give hints. After 3 minutes, cold-call 4 learners (one per group) for their fraction estimate. Record responses verbatim (e.g., '1/4 of the sector', '½', 'about 30%') in a T-chart on the board labelled 'Our Predictions'. Teacher then says: 'Keep these predictions visible — we will return to them at the end of Phase 2 to see who was closest.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Journaling with Public Commitment: by writing and then publicly sharing a numerical estimate before any instruction, learners activate prior knowledge of sector area and create cognitive dissonance when they realise they lack a method to handle the curved boundary — directly mirroring the puzzle the Wakulima Market customer faces. This primes them to attend purposefully to the subtraction strategy in Phase 2.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: every learner has a written numerical estimate (fraction or percentage) and a written sentence of reasoning in their notebook before Phase 2 begins. Teacher scans for misconceptions — particularly learners who write 'segment area = ½ × sector area regardless of θ', flagging those groups for targeted questioning during Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives: (a) their labelled sector cut-outs from previous lessons; (b) a ruler and a pencil; (c) a printed Group Data Table (columns: θ°, r cm, chord length c cm, sector area cm², triangle area ½r²sinθ cm², segment area cm²). Step 1 (5 min): Using a ruler, learners draw the chord connecting the two ends of the arc on their sector cut-out, then cut along the chord to physically separate the triangular piece from the curved segment. Both pieces are labelled and kept. Step 2 (5 min): Learners measure the chord length c, verify the radius r = 18 cm, and record. Step 3 (5 min): Groups calculate the area of the triangle using the formula ½r²sinθ (introduced in Sub-Strand 2.4 Area of Polygons — teacher reminds learners this is the 'two-sides-and-included-angle' formula they already know). They record sector area (calculated in a previous lesson) and compute: Segment area = Sector area − Triangle area. Step 4 (3 min): Groups compare their computed segment area to their original prediction from Phase 1 and note the difference in their notebooks.
framework.teacherMoves: Before learners begin cutting, teacher models the procedure ONCE using a large demonstration cut-out on the board: 'I draw my chord here — joining the two points where the radii meet the arc. I cut along the chord. Now I have two pieces: the triangle [holds up triangle] and the segment [holds up curved sliver]. I want the area of THIS piece [holds up segment].' Pause 10 seconds. 'How can I get it if I already know the sector area?' Wait 12 seconds for think time, then cold-call 2 learners. Guide toward the subtraction idea without stating it directly. Circulate during group work. At the 8-minute mark, stop all groups briefly: 'Check: has everyone used ½r²sinθ for the triangle — not ½ × base × height? Why do we use ½r²sinθ here?' Cold-call 1 learner. At the 13-minute mark prompt groups: 'Compare your answer to your Phase 1 prediction. How far off were you? Write one sentence about WHY you were off or right.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete Manipulation with Data Recording: physically cutting the triangle from the sector makes the subtraction relationship tangible and irreversible in learners' minds. Recording both pieces' areas in the same table column-by-column scaffolds the algebraic relationship (Segment = Sector − Triangle) as a pattern across four different angle values, not merely a one-off formula. This connects directly to the phenomenon: each watermelon slice the vendor cuts has both a sector area and a triangular-central portion, and the curved rind piece alone is the segment.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each group's Data Table has all six columns populated with correct units (cm²) for all four θ values. Teacher checks specifically that the triangle area column uses ½r²sinθ (not ½ × base × height from a measurement), and that segment area values are smaller than sector area values — a necessary logical check. Groups whose segment area exceeds sector area are immediately redirected.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Formula Derivation (8 min): Each group writes the general formula on a large sheet of manila paper: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. They factor it as ½r²[(θπ/180) − sinθ] and annotate each term in a different colour, labelling what it represents physically (sector portion vs. triangle portion). They verify the formula using their own measured values (r = 18 cm, θ = 90°) and confirm it matches their cut-and-subtract result. Part B — Wakulima Market Verdict (10 min): Groups receive the 'Customer Complaint Card': 'Mama Wanjiku at Wakulima Market cut a circular watermelon (r = 18 cm) into four unequal wedge-shaped pieces. The central angles were: Piece A = 40°, Piece B = 65°, Piece C = 90°, Piece D = 120°. She then cut a chord across each piece and sold ONLY the curved segment to each customer, keeping the triangular centres to make juice. Customer Ochieng (Piece D) complained that Customer Auma (Piece C) received a larger segment even though Ochieng's angle was bigger. Was Ochieng right?' Groups calculate all four segment areas and write a one-paragraph verdict with supporting calculations. Part C — Connections (4 min): Groups identify two additional real-life contexts in Kenya where segment area matters (suggested: the area of land irrigated by a pivot-irrigation system beyond a fence line in Rift Valley; the area of a decorative tile pattern at a Mombasa hotel).
framework.teacherMoves: For Part A, teacher writes on the board: 'Sector area = (θ/360)πr². Triangle area = ½r²sinθ. Therefore, Segment area = ?' and waits 10 seconds before taking responses. Cold-call 2 learners to complete the subtraction. Teacher then says: 'Factor out ½r² from both terms. What do you get?' Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner. Write the factored form alongside the expanded form — tell learners both are correct and acceptable in assessments. For Part B, circulate and prompt groups that are stuck: 'First calculate sector area for Piece D. Then calculate triangle area for Piece D. Now subtract. Does the result surprise you?' After 10 minutes, cold-call one group to present their verdict. If the verdict is correct (Ochieng is partially right — Piece D segment IS larger than Piece C segment), ask: 'Why did the segment areas NOT increase in the same proportion as the angles? What role does sinθ play?' Wait 15 seconds — this is a high-cognitive-demand question. Accept reasoning rather than a precise answer. For Part C, cold-call 2 different groups for their Kenyan contexts. Explicitly connect each back to the driving question: 'So the answer to our driving question now includes segments, not just sectors.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Writing: the Customer Complaint Card requires learners to state a claim (Ochieng is right/wrong), support it with numerical evidence (four segment area calculations), and explain their reasoning (relationship between θ, sinθ, and segment area). This is a full scientific argument structure applied to a mathematics context, directly answering the driving question with real numbers from the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each group's manila paper shows (1) the formula with colour-coded annotations, (2) a numerical verification using r = 18 cm and their own θ, and (3) a written verdict paragraph with all four segment areas calculated to 1 decimal place. Teacher listens for learners correctly interpreting why sinθ grows more slowly than θ for large angles — this nuanced reasoning distinguishes 'Meets Expectations' from 'Exceeds Expectations' on the KICD rubric.

framework.learnerExperience: The full Driving Question Board (DQB), built incrementally across all 8 lessons, is displayed at the front of the room. Each group receives three sticky-note colours: GREEN = 'We can now answer this fully', YELLOW = 'We can answer this partially', RED = 'Still puzzling us'. Groups spend 4 minutes silently reviewing every card on the DQB and deciding on a colour for each question their group originally posted. Groups then send one representative to the board to re-label cards. The class reviews any remaining RED cards (if any) and attempts a brief collective answer. The teacher reads the original Driving Question aloud one final time: 'How can we calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped or segment-shaped piece of a circle — like a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market — so that we can solve fair-sharing and design problems in real life?' The whole class co-constructs a one-sentence Final Answer on the board, and every learner copies it into their notebook.
framework.teacherMoves: Teacher points to the DQB and says: 'This board has been our map across 8 lessons. Let's see how much of it we can now colour green.' Give groups 4 minutes of quiet review time — do not answer questions during this time; redirect all queries back to group discussion. After 4 minutes, invite representatives to re-label cards. Stand back and observe — do not direct placement. After all groups have labelled, scan the board and say: 'I see [X] green cards, [Y] yellow cards, [Z] red cards. Let's look at any remaining red cards together.' If red cards remain (expected: at most 1–2 extension-level questions), facilitate a 2-minute class discussion. Then ask: 'In one sentence — using the words RADIUS, ANGLE, SECTOR, SEGMENT, and FORMULA — can someone complete this starter: The exact area of any wedge or segment of a circle can be calculated by…?' Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner, then invite additions from 2 more peers. Write the agreed sentence on the board in a box titled 'OUR FINAL ANSWER'. Learners copy it.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Audit with Colour Coding: revisiting every question posted throughout the unit with a traffic-light system makes the progression of understanding visible and metacognitive. Learners experience closure — a rare and motivating feeling in mathematics — while the constraint of using five specific vocabulary words in the Final Answer forces precise scientific language rather than vague summary.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: at least 80% of DQB cards are marked GREEN by the end of Phase 4. Teacher records the specific cards marked YELLOW or RED as evidence of residual gaps to address in revision or the next sub-strand. Every learner's notebook contains the agreed Final Answer sentence, which serves as a portable exit reference.

framework.learnerExperience: Model Revision (10 min): Learners open their notebooks to their Lesson 1 naïve model — the drawing they made at the very start of the unit showing 'what they thought determined the size of a watermelon slice'. Each learner individually annotates their original Lesson 1 model in RED pen, adding: (a) the sector area formula with labels; (b) the triangle area formula with labels; (c) the segment area formula with labels; (d) an arrow from the 'angle' in the diagram labelled 'THIS is what changes the area — not just how it looks'. Below the revised model, learners write a 'Then vs. Now' statement: 'At the start of this unit I thought… Now I know…'. Gallery Walk (10 min): Each group posts their manila paper (from Phase 3) and their Group Data Table on the classroom wall. Groups rotate around the room (2 minutes per station) leaving one sticky-note comment per station using the sentence starter: 'One thing this group's work helped me understand about the watermelon puzzle is…'. The lesson closes with the teacher reading 3–4 sticky-note comments aloud and asking the whole class: 'Has Mama Wanjiku at Wakulima Market been treating her customers fairly? What would you tell her to do differently, using mathematics?'
framework.teacherMoves: For the Model Revision, say: 'Open to your Lesson 1 model. Look at it carefully. In RED pen, add everything you now know that your Lesson 1 self did not know. You have 10 minutes — no talking, this is individual work.' Circulate and look specifically for learners who only add formulas without annotating the diagram — prompt these learners: 'Can you point to WHERE in your drawing the angle θ lives? Where is r? Where would the chord go to create a segment?' For the Gallery Walk, set a visible timer for 2-minute rotations. Insist on the sentence starter — do not accept 'good job' style comments. After the Gallery Walk, read 3–4 sticky notes aloud and ask: 'What would you tell Mama Wanjiku?' Wait 10 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners. Aim for a response that includes a specific recommendation (e.g., 'She should cut all wedges at the same central angle, or advertise the area in cm² on a price board so customers can compare'). Close by saying: 'You have just done what mathematicians and market inspectors do — you used exact measurement to replace guessing with fairness. That is the power of area of part of a circle.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Then-vs-Now Model Comparison with Peer Gallery Walk: comparing the Lesson 1 naïve model to the fully annotated final model makes conceptual growth concrete and visible — a key metacognitive practice in CBE. The Gallery Walk distributes the explanatory load across all groups, allowing learners to encounter four different worked examples and articulate what each contributed to their understanding of the driving question. The final 'advice to Mama Wanjiku' question requires learners to translate mathematical knowledge into a practical, Kenya-grounded recommendation — completing the full sense-making cycle from phenomenon to formula to application.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each learner's revised model contains all three formulae with labelled diagrams and a complete 'Then vs. Now' statement of at least two sentences. Teacher collects the Group Data Tables as a summative artefact for the Observation Schedule assessment method (KICD Appendix 1). The 'advice to Mama Wanjiku' responses are used as an oral exit check — learners who cannot connect the formula to a practical recommendation are identified for follow-up in the next lesson's opening review.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your journal:
1. FORMULA DERIVATION: Did all groups successfully derive Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ independently, or did some groups require the subtraction idea to be prompted? If prompting was needed, which step (isolating the triangle vs. applying ½r²sinθ) caused the most difficulty? How will this inform your instruction in Sub-Strand 2.6 (Surface Area of Solids) where similar composite-shape strategies apply?
2. CUSTOMER COMPLAINT CARD: Were learners able to correctly interpret why Piece D (θ = 120°) has a larger segment area than Piece C (θ = 90°), and articulate the role of sinθ? If learners simply said 'bigger angle = bigger segment' without unpacking the sinθ term, note this as a gap in algebraic reasoning to address during revision.
3. DQB AUDIT: How many cards remained RED or YELLOW at the end? Were these extension questions posted by high-attaining learners, or foundational questions from learners who still struggled with the core formulae? Use this evidence to plan differentiated revision activities.
4. MODEL COMPARISON: Did learners' 'Then vs. Now' statements show genuine conceptual growth, or did they simply copy formulas without articulating a change in understanding? Select 3–4 representative notebooks (one from each attainment band) and use these as evidence in your portfolio for peer-learning discussions.
5. EQUITY AND FAIRNESS: The watermelon phenomenon was designed to connect mathematics to fairness and social justice — core values in the KICD framework. Did learners make this connection explicitly in their 'advice to Mama Wanjiku' responses? If not, how might you embed values-based connections more explicitly in future capstone lessons?
6. TIMING: The lesson is planned for 80 minutes. Note which phase ran over or under time and adjust the Observation Schedule assessment to be completed outside class if the Gallery Walk was rushed.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Essential Mathematics – Grade 10 | Sub-strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation document. Your goal is to write a complete, well-organised answer to the driving question using everything you have learned across all 8 lessons. Read the driving question carefully, then use each section below as a building block for your full explanation. Write in full sentences and paragraphs. Show all working where calculations are required. Use diagrams where they help your explanation. A model exemplar answer is provided in each section — study it, then write your own response in your own words and using your own examples.

sections.title: Section 1: Anchor Your Explanation to the Phenomenon
sections.prompt: Start by explaining the real-world puzzle that launched this unit. Describe what is happening at Wakulima Market and why the mama mboga's watermelon slices look so different in size even when they all come from the same circular melon. What is the key variable that controls how big each wedge is? Why can't we use the area formulas we already know — for rectangles, triangles, or other polygons — to solve this problem directly?
sections.exemplar: At Wakulima Market in Nairobi, a mama mboga cuts a large circular watermelon into wedge-shaped slices to sell by the piece. Even though every slice comes from the same melon — meaning every slice shares the same radius — customers notice that some pieces look much bigger than others. The key variable is the angle of the cut. A wide cut creates a large wedge; a narrow cut creates a thin sliver. This is puzzling because our earlier area formulas (for rectangles, triangles, and polygons) only work for shapes bounded by straight sides. A watermelon wedge is bounded by two straight radii AND a curved arc (part of the circle's circumference), so none of our old formulas apply directly. We need a new approach that accounts for the curved boundary and the size of the central angle.

sections.title: Section 2: Define the Key Terms and Shapes
sections.prompt: Clearly define each of the following terms and support each definition with a labelled sketch or a real-life example from the Kenyan context: (a) Sector, (b) Segment, (c) Arc, (d) Central angle (in both degrees and radians), (e) Minor vs. major sector. Explain the difference between a sector and a segment — many students confuse these two shapes.
sections.exemplar: A sector is the 'wedge' shape formed by two radii and the arc between them — like one slice of the watermelon. A segment is the region between a chord (a straight cut that does NOT pass through the centre) and the arc it cuts off — like the rind-edge piece left over if you cut straight across rather than through the centre. An arc is the curved part of the circle's boundary between two points. The central angle is the angle at the centre of the circle formed by the two radii; it can be measured in degrees (e.g., 90°) or in radians (e.g., π/2 rad). A minor sector has a central angle less than 180° (a small slice), while a major sector has a central angle greater than 180° (more than half the melon). The easiest way to remember the difference between a sector and a segment: a sector always includes the centre point of the circle; a segment never includes the centre point.

sections.title: Section 3: Derive and Apply the Area Formulas
sections.prompt: Explain WHERE the formula for the area of a sector comes from — do not just state it. Show how it is derived from the area of a full circle. Then write the formula in BOTH degree form and radian form. Finally, show a fully worked example using realistic Kenyan numbers: a watermelon with radius 21 cm is cut into a sector with a central angle of 60°. Calculate the exact area of that slice. Then show how to find the area of a segment by combining the sector formula with the area of a triangle.
sections.exemplar:
A full circle has area A = πr². A full circle also has a central angle of 360°. A sector is simply a fraction of the full circle — the fraction is (θ/360) when θ is in degrees. Therefore:

Area of sector (degrees) = (θ/360) × πr²

In radian form, because a full circle = 2π radians, the fraction becomes (θ/2π), giving:

Area of sector (radians) = ½r²θ

Both formulas express the same idea: the sector's area is proportional to its central angle.

Worked Example — Watermelon Slice:
Radius r = 21 cm, central angle θ = 60°
Area of sector = (60/360) × π × 21²
= (1/6) × π × 441
= 441π/6
= 73.5π
≈ 230.9 cm²

So one 60° slice of the watermelon covers approximately 230.9 cm².

Area of a Segment:
A segment = sector − triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.
Area of triangle = ½r²sin θ
Area of segment = ½r²θ − ½r²sin θ = ½r²(θ − sin θ) [θ in radians]

For the same watermelon (r = 21 cm, θ = 60° = π/3 rad):
Area of segment = ½ × 21² × (π/3 − sin 60°)
= ½ × 441 × (1.047 − 0.866)
= 220.5 × 0.181
≈ 39.9 cm²

This tells us how much watermelon flesh lies between the straight chord cut and the curved rind.

sections.title: Section 4: Answer the Driving Question Directly
sections.prompt: Now answer the driving question fully and directly. Explain how you can calculate the EXACT area of any sector or segment shape. Then explain how this knowledge solves the fair-sharing problem at Wakulima Market. If the mama mboga wants every customer to receive exactly the same area of watermelon, what must she control? Use mathematics to support your answer. Include at least one example showing that two slices with DIFFERENT angles from the SAME melon have DIFFERENT areas, proving that angle alone explains the size difference.
sections.exemplar:
We can calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped sector using the formula: Area = (θ/360) × πr², where θ is the central angle in degrees and r is the radius of the circle. For a segment, we subtract the triangle: Area = ½r²(θ − sin θ) with θ in radians.

This directly solves the Wakulima Market puzzle. The mama mboga's slices look different because she is cutting at different central angles. Since all slices come from the same melon (same r), the ONLY variable that changes the area is θ.

Proof with numbers (r = 21 cm):
• Slice A: θ = 40° → Area = (40/360) × π × 441 = 49π ≈ 153.9 cm²
• Slice B: θ = 80° → Area = (80/360) × π × 441 = 98π ≈ 307.9 cm²

Slice B is exactly TWICE the size of Slice A, even though both come from the same melon. Doubling the angle doubles the area — they are directly proportional.

For a truly fair share: if the melon has a full angle of 360° and the mama mboga wants to give n customers equal slices, each slice must have a central angle of (360° ÷ n). For 8 customers: 360° ÷ 8 = 45° per slice. Each slice would have area = (45/360) × π × 21² = (1/8) × 441π ≈ 173.2 cm². Mathematics gives the mama mboga — and every customer — a guarantee of fairness.

sections.title: Section 5: Extend to Design and Real-Life Applications
sections.prompt: Go beyond the market. Describe at least TWO other real-life situations in Kenya where calculating the area of a sector or segment is genuinely useful. For each situation, identify the shape (sector or segment?), state what r and θ represent in that context, and explain what the calculated area tells us. Then reflect: What is the most important mathematical idea you are taking away from this unit, and how has it changed the way you think about curved shapes in the world around you?
sections.exemplar:
Application 1 — Irrigation Pivot Farming in the Rift Valley:
In large-scale farms near Nakuru, centre-pivot irrigation systems rotate around a fixed water source and spray water in a circular arc. If a pivot arm of length 80 m rotates through an angle of 120°, the irrigated area is a sector: Area = (120/360) × π × 80² = (1/3) × π × 6400 ≈ 6702 m². A farmer needs this calculation to know how many bags of fertiliser to apply and whether the water supply is sufficient for that exact area of crops.

Application 2 — Designing a Kenyan Craft Fan or Kikoy Pattern:
Artisans in Mombasa and Kisumu design decorative fans and woven kikoy borders using repeating sector and segment patterns. A designer creating a fan that opens to 150° with a radius of 30 cm needs the sector area to estimate fabric cost: Area = (150/360) × π × 30² ≈ 1178.1 cm². Accurate costing depends on this calculation.

Reflection:
The most important idea from this unit is that area is proportional to angle when the radius stays fixed. Before this unit, curved boundaries felt impossible to measure exactly. Now I understand that a circle is just a shape whose parts can be unlocked by treating the central angle as a fraction of the whole 360°. Every arc, every wedge, every segment becomes calculable — and that makes the curved world around us just as measurable as the straight-edged world we started with.

Both degree and radian forms are stated. All worked calculations are correct, fully shown step by step, and include correct units (cm²).

The answer is logically structured and mathematically convincing.

rubric.developing: The student identifies only one application or the applications given are not distinctly Kenyan or realistic. Calculations may be missing or incorrect. The reflection restates what was done rather than identifying a transferable mathematical idea.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 2.5: Area of Part of a Circle
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How can we calculate the exact area of any wedge-shaped or segment-shaped piece of a circle — like a watermelon slice at Wakulima Market — so that we can solve fair-sharing and design problems in real life?

lessons.title: Introducing the Circle and Its Parts
lessons.observed: Students examined physical circular objects (bottle caps, sufuria lids, round chapati) and identified key parts: centre, radius, diameter, circumference, chord, arc, sector, and segment. Teacher should cold-call at least 4 students to label parts on a large circle drawn on the board. Allow 30-second wait time after each prompt.
lessons.learned: A circle is a set of all points equidistant from a fixed centre. Its key measurable parts — radius (r), diameter (d = 2r), and circumference (C = 2πr or πd) — form the foundation for calculating any area within the circle. Students should be able to distinguish between a sector (wedge bounded by two radii and an arc) and a segment (region between a chord and an arc).
lessons.explained: Teachers should explain that every part of a circle is defined by its relationship to the radius. Emphasise that the watermelon slice at Wakulima Market is a real-world sector — bounded by two straight cuts (radii) and a curved rind (arc). Pedagogical note: use the analogy of cutting a round chapati — each cut from the centre outward creates a sector. This anchors the driving question from Lesson 1 and gives students a mental image to carry through all 8 lessons.

lessons.title: Reviewing Circle Area and Introducing the Central Angle
lessons.observed: Students reviewed the formula for the area of a full circle (A = πr²) using concrete examples — e.g., a circular shamba plot of radius 7 m near Kericho. They then measured central angles of pre-drawn sectors using protractors and recorded the angle and the fraction it represents of 360°. Teacher should circulate and prompt: 'If the full circle is 360°, what fraction of the circle is your sector?'
lessons.learned: The area of a full circle is A = πr². A central angle θ (in degrees) describes what fraction (θ/360) of the full circle a sector occupies. This fraction is the critical link between the full circle area and any sector area. Students must be fluent in expressing angles as fractions of 360° before moving to the sector formula in Lesson 3.
lessons.explained: Teachers should emphasise that 360° represents one complete revolution — a full circle. Any sector is simply a proportional slice of that full circle. Pedagogical note: draw a pie chart of a family's ugali-and-sukuma wiki meal portions on the board. Ask: 'If ugali takes up 180° of the pie chart, what fraction of the meal is it?' This proportional reasoning is the conceptual engine of the entire sub-strand. Cold-call 3 students to state the fraction for angles of 90°, 120°, and 45° before closing the lesson.

lessons.title: Investigating Sector Area with Cut-Outs
lessons.observed: Students cut out full circles from paper, folded or divided them into sectors of known angles (e.g., 90°, 60°, 120°), and physically compared sector areas by stacking and overlapping cut-outs. They recorded findings in a table: central angle | fraction of circle | predicted area | calculated area. Teacher should ask: 'What do you notice when you double the angle?' Allow 45 seconds of think time before taking responses from at least 3 students.
lessons.learned: The area of a sector is directly proportional to its central angle. Doubling the central angle exactly doubles the sector area, confirming the relationship A = (θ/360) × πr². A 180° sector has exactly half the circle's area; a 90° sector has exactly one quarter. This proportional relationship is precise and exact, not an approximation.
lessons.explained: Teachers should use the cut-out activity results to guide students to generalise: 'If a 360° sector has area πr², then a θ° sector has area (θ/360) × πr².' Pedagogical note: stress that this is not a new formula to memorise in isolation — it is a direct application of proportional reasoning students already know. Connect back to the driving question: 'A watermelon slice cut at 60° from the centre — what fraction of the whole watermelon face does it represent?' Ensure students record the formula A = (θ/360) × πr² in their notes with units clearly labelled (cm², m²).

lessons.title: Cutting Watermelon Fairly: Deriving the Area of a Sector Formula
lessons.observed: Students worked through a structured scenario: a round watermelon of radius 15 cm is cut into slices at Wakulima Market. Each vendor cuts at a different angle. Students calculated sector areas for angles of 45°, 60°, 90°, and 120° and compared results. Teacher should pose: 'Which vendor gives the customer the biggest slice per shilling?' Cold-call 4 students to present their calculations. Require units in every answer.
lessons.learned: Area of sector = (θ/360) × πr². A 90° sector contains exactly one-quarter of the total circle area. The formula works for any angle and any radius. Students also learned that 'fair sharing' requires equal central angles — not just equal-looking cuts — because area scales with angle. This is a key insight connecting mathematics to real-life equity and commerce at Kenyan markets.
lessons.explained: Teachers should formalise the derivation: (θ/360) × πr² emerges because the sector is the fraction θ/360 of the full circle of area πr². Pedagogical note: ask students to consider what happens if a market vendor cuts a 'bigger-looking' slice by increasing the radius rather than the angle — does this change the angle-based formula? This deepens understanding that both r and θ independently affect sector area. Emphasise that the formula is exact, not an estimate, when π is used symbolically.

lessons.title: Applying the Sector Area Formula to Real-Life Problems
lessons.observed: Students solved a set of applied problems involving sectors in Kenyan contexts: irrigated fan-shaped farm plots in the Rift Valley, a rotating sprinkler covering a 120° arc, a Nairobi roundabout garden in the shape of a sector, and a clock hand sweeping a sector in a given time. Teacher should circulate and use targeted questioning: 'What is your r? What is your θ? Have you checked your units?' Require at least one self-correction per group before submitting answers.
lessons.learned: The formula A = (θ/360) × πr² applies directly to any real-world sector problem once the radius and central angle are correctly identified from the context. Students learned to extract r and θ from word problems, apply the formula, and express answers in appropriate units (cm², m², hectares where relevant). They also practised working with π ≈ 22/7 and π ≈ 3.14 and leaving answers in terms of π.
lessons.explained: Teachers should highlight common errors: confusing radius with diameter (e.g., a watermelon described as '30 cm across' has r = 15 cm), and using the wrong angle (e.g., using the arc length angle instead of the central angle). Pedagogical note: display a worked example on the board using the Rift Valley irrigation scenario step-by-step, then erase selective steps and cold-call students to reconstruct the solution. This retrieval practice consolidates procedural fluency before moving to segment area in Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Formalising the Sector Area Formula: From Watermelon Wedges to Irrigation Arcs
lessons.observed: Students revisited their Lesson 3 and 4 findings and formally recorded the sector area formula with a derivation narrative. They then applied the formula to a design task: planning a fan-shaped irrigation arc for a maize farm in Eldoret, given fixed pipe length (radius) and available land angle. Students sketched and labelled their sectors and computed areas. Teacher should ask: 'How does changing the pipe length by 2 m change the irrigated area?' Allow 60 seconds of paired discussion before cold-calling.
lessons.learned: Learners confirmed that the area of any sector is a proportional fraction of the full circle's area: A = (θ/360) × πr². They also discovered that because r is squared in the formula, small increases in radius produce large increases in area — a non-linear relationship. A 10% increase in radius increases sector area by approximately 21%. This has practical implications for irrigation and land-use planning.
lessons.explained: Teachers should make the r² effect explicit by comparing two worked examples side by side: one where θ doubles and one where r doubles. Students should see that doubling θ doubles the area (linear), while doubling r quadruples the area (quadratic). Pedagogical note: connect this to the driving question by asking, 'If a watermelon vendor doubles the slice angle versus doubles the watermelon size, which gives the customer more area?' This is a rich discussion prompt. Ensure students update their exercise books with a fully labelled formula box before Lesson 7.

lessons.title: Investigating Segment Area: From Sector to Slice — Unlocking the Curved Piece
lessons.observed: Students physically cut a sector from a paper circle, then drew the chord connecting the two endpoints of the arc to create a triangle inside the sector. They cut out the triangle and placed it aside, leaving only the segment (the 'rind piece'). They recorded: Area of segment = Area of sector − Area of triangle. Teacher should ask: 'What shape is the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord?' Wait 30 seconds, then cold-call 3 students. Guide students to confirm it is an isosceles triangle with two sides equal to r.
lessons.learned: The area of a circular segment = area of sector − area of the isosceles triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. The triangle has area = ½r²sinθ (derived from the formula for area of a triangle using two sides and an included angle). Therefore: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. Students must be able to identify θ as the central angle of both the sector and the triangle's included angle.
lessons.explained: Teachers should carefully derive ½r²sinθ: the triangle has two sides of length r and included angle θ, so Area of triangle = ½ × r × r × sin θ = ½r²sinθ. Pedagogical note: many students confuse the triangle's base-height formula with this sine version — emphasise that we use the sine formula here because we know two sides and the included angle, not the base and perpendicular height directly. Use a numerical example: r = 10 cm, θ = 60°, so triangle area = ½ × 100 × sin60° = 50 × (√3/2) = 25√3 cm². Connect to the driving question: 'The curved rind piece of a watermelon slice is a segment — now we can find its exact area.'

lessons.title: Segment Area, Final Explanation & Fair-Share Verdict — Completing the Watermelon Puzzle
lessons.observed: Students solved the culminating problem: a round watermelon at Wakulima Market has radius 18 cm. Three friends each take a slice cut at 80° from the centre. Using both the sector and segment formulas, they calculated (a) the area of each wedge-shaped sector slice, (b) the area of just the curved segment (the 'rind portion'), and (c) whether the three slices together cover more or less than half the watermelon face. Teacher should cold-call one student per sub-question to present to the class. Require justification for every numerical answer.
lessons.learned: Learners derived and applied the complete formula: Area of segment = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. They verified it numerically against their cut-and-subtract results from Lesson 7, confirming the algebraic and physical methods agree. They also applied the sector formula to confirm that three 80° slices cover 240° — exactly two-thirds of the watermelon face. The driving question is fully answered: exact area calculations enable fair sharing and precise design decisions in real-life Kenyan contexts.
lessons.explained: Teachers should lead a full summary discussion connecting all 8 lessons: (1) circle parts → (2) central angles as fractions → (3–6) sector area A = (θ/360)πr² → (7–8) segment area = sector − triangle = (θ/360)πr² − ½r²sinθ. Pedagogical note: draw a single diagram on the board showing a watermelon slice with all labels (r, θ, sector, triangle, segment) and annotate each formula on the diagram. Ask the class: 'How would a market vendor use this to price slices fairly?' Allow open discussion for 3 minutes. Close by having students write a one-sentence answer to the driving question in their own words — this serves as both a formative assessment and a personal record of their learning journey.
